pages.title: Desktop app updates
pages.description: How the Lumen desktop app checks for, verifies and installs updates, and what it sends.
pages.md:
The desktop app (Windows, macOS, Linux) updates itself from the project's
GitHub releases.

- **Check:** command palette → **Check for updates…**. A stable build never
  checks on its own. A beta build checks once a day at launch, unless you
  turn that off under [feature flags](/getting-started/beta/).
- **Channel:** command palette → **Update channel: switch between stable and beta** switches between stable
  and beta releases ([beta channel](/getting-started/beta/)).
- **What is sent:** one request to the release server with the app version
  and platform. No notes, no account, no identifier. It appears in the
  privacy log.
- **Local only:** when the privacy policy is *local only*, nothing is
  checked. The command says so instead.
- **Verification:** every update is signed. The app checks the signature
  against the key built into it and refuses a file that doesn't match, or an
  older version presented as new.
- **Install:** after you confirm, Lumen downloads, verifies, installs and restarts.

A build without the update key (local and development builds) has no
updater. *Check for updates…* says it isn't configured, and new versions are
installed by hand.

## Signed installers

Release installers are code-signed once the project's signing certificates
are in place (Windows Authenticode, Apple Developer ID). Until then Windows
SmartScreen and macOS Gatekeeper show a warning on first launch.

## What the app is allowed to do

The window has no general file-system permission. It reaches only the vault
folder you picked, through Lumen's own commands. No shell, no arbitrary
HTTP from the native side, and no source maps in the shipped files.

pages.title: Send feedback
pages.description: Report a bug, an idea or a question as a GitHub issue or as text to copy. Lumen has no feedback server, and nothing is sent until you click.
pages.md:
Open it with `⌘K → Help: Send feedback`, or with **Report a problem…** at the
bottom of the [AI doctor](/ai/doctor/).

Lumen has no feedback server. The form turns what you write into the text of
a GitHub issue, and you choose what happens to it:

- **Open on GitHub** opens github.com in a new tab with the issue form filled
  in (title, text and a label for the kind). You check it there and submit it.
  You need a GitHub account.
- **Copy text** puts the same text on your clipboard, for an e-mail or
  anywhere else.

Until you click one of those two buttons, nothing leaves your device. The form
makes no network request, and the preview shows exactly the text that will be
sent.

## What goes in

| Part | When | What |
|---|---|---|
| Kind, title, description | always | what you wrote |
| App and browser details | ticked (the default) | Lumen version; web, installed app or desktop; platform; language; AI policy; the browser's user agent |
| AI doctor report | only when you tick it | the doctor's checks of the local AI stack. It never contains note text. Keys, tokens, passwords in URLs and e-mail addresses are removed before it goes in. |
| Screenshot | only when you take one | never part of the text (see below) |

If the issue text is too long for a link, GitHub opens with the title only and
the text is on your clipboard: paste it into the issue.

## Screenshots

**Save a screenshot to attach** asks your browser to capture a screen, window or
tab. The browser shows its own prompt, so you choose what is captured. The
picture is saved on your computer as `lumen-feedback-<date>-<time>.png`. It is
not uploaded. Attach it to the GitHub issue yourself. It may show your notes,
so look at it first.

Browsers without screen capture (most phones) say so and skip this step.

## Diagnostics file

**Save diagnostics** (in the feedback form, on an error screen, or **Save a
diagnostics file** in the command palette) saves `lumen-diagnostics-<date>.json`
on your computer, for you to attach to the issue. It holds what a maintainer
needs to understand a problem, and nothing about what you wrote:

- the version, the app shell (web, installed, desktop), the platform and
  the browser;
- your settings, copied one by one from a fixed list: switches, modes and
  sizes. No note names, folders, keys, tokens or e-mail addresses;
- the vault counted, not read: how many notes, other files and folders, and
  their total size;
- storage: whether the vault is in the browser's private storage, and how
  full it is;
- the last warnings and errors, with every path, URL path, quoted text,
  address and key in them replaced by a placeholder.

Before the file is saved, Lumen checks it once more against the text it
holds in memory (your notes, their names, your keys), and refuses to save a
file that would contain any of it.

## Help in the app

**Help** in the command palette (or F1) opens this documentation inside
Lumen. It is packed into the app, so it works offline, and its search
handles Hebrew prefixes as the website's search does. Every panel and
dialog has a **?** button that opens the help at the part about it.

pages.title: Moving from Bear
pages.description: Export Bear notes as Markdown and bring them, with their images, into Lumen.
pages.md:
## Export from Bear

1. Select the notes (or **⌘A** in a tag).
2. **File → Export Notes…**, format **Markdown**, with **Export attachments**
   on. Bear writes one `.md` file per note and a folder of images next to
   each.

## Bring it in

Zip the export folder, or keep it as a folder, then
`⌘K → Import notes from another app (Obsidian, Notion, Evernote, Bear, Keep, Logseq, OneNote…)…`. The notes and
their images go into a new folder, `Imported/<name>`, with the image links
intact.

## What changes

| In Bear | In Lumen |
|---|---|
| `#tags` and `#nested/tags` | the same inline tags; the tags panel lists them |
| `#multi word tags#` | write them as `#multi-word-tags` (Lumen tags have no spaces) |
| `::highlight::` | kept as text; Markdown has no highlight (use **bold**, or `{==highlight==}` in suggesting mode) |
| `[[note links]]` | the same syntax |
| Sync between devices | Bear's iCloud sync does not reach Lumen; use Git or a shared folder |

pages.title: Moving from Evernote
pages.description: Get your notebooks out of Evernote and into Lumen as Markdown, with their images and attachments.
pages.md:
Evernote keeps notes in its own format (ENML), so they are converted on the
way in.

## Export from Evernote

1. Select a notebook (or the notes you want).
2. **File → Export notes…** (or **⋯ → Export**).

## Bring it in

:::note[Coming with the import wizard]
The import wizard (plan W1.26) reads `.enex` exports directly: one folder
per notebook, images and files in place, to-dos as tasks, tags and the
creation and edit dates as properties. Until it ships in your version, use
the HTML route below.
:::

**HTML route**: export the notes as **HTML** (one file per note). In Lumen,
open each file (`⌘O`) or drop it on the window — the HTML is converted to
Markdown, images included — and save it to your vault.

## What changes

| In Evernote | In Lumen |
|---|---|
| Notebooks and stacks | folders |
| Tags | `tags:` in each note's frontmatter |
| Checklists | Markdown tasks `- [ ]` |
| Encrypted text | stays out (Evernote does not export it in the clear) |
| Reminders, sharing | not in the export |

pages.title: Moving from Google Docs
pages.description: Turn Google Docs into Markdown notes in Lumen — one document, or a whole Drive folder.
pages.md:
## One document

1. In Google Docs: **File → Download → Markdown (.md)**. Older documents
   can also be downloaded as **Word (.docx)**.
2. In Lumen: open the file (`⌘O`) or drop it on the window. A `.md` file
   opens as it is; a `.docx` is converted to Markdown with its headings,
   lists, tables and images.
3. Save it into your vault.

## A whole folder

Google Takeout (takeout.google.com → **Drive**) exports a folder of
documents as `.docx`. Unzip it, and open the files in Lumen one by one, or
convert them in bulk to Markdown first and import the folder with
`⌘K → Import notes from another app (Obsidian, Notion, Evernote, Bear, Keep, Logseq, OneNote…)…`.

## What changes

| In Google Docs | In Lumen |
|---|---|
| Headings, lists, tables, links | Markdown headings, lists, tables, links |
| Comments and suggestions | not in the download; Lumen has its own [suggesting mode and comments](/collab/webrtc/) |
| Right-to-left paragraphs | detected per paragraph — see [Hebrew and right-to-left](/editor/hebrew/) |
| Sharing | Lumen is local-first; see [real-time collaboration](/collab/webrtc/) |

pages.title: Moving from Notion
pages.description: Export a Notion workspace and bring its pages, links and attachments into Lumen.
pages.md:
## Export from Notion

1. In Notion: **Settings → Export** (a single page: **⋯ → Export**).
2. Choose **Markdown & CSV**, include subpages, and download the .zip.

## Bring it in

`⌘K → Import notes from another app (Obsidian, Notion, Evernote, Bear, Keep, Logseq, OneNote…)…`, then pick the
.zip as it came. Lumen recognises a Notion export by the 32-character IDs
Notion adds to every file name, and:

- removes the IDs from file and folder names (`Plans 1a2b….md` → `Plans.md`);
- rewrites the links between pages to the new names, keeping `#headings`;
- numbers two pages that end up with the same name (`Page 2.md`) and keeps
  the links pointing at the right one;
- imports everything into a new folder, `Imported/<name>`, never over an
  existing note.

## What changes

| In Notion | In Lumen |
|---|---|
| Pages and subpages | Markdown files and folders |
| Databases | a `.csv` per database, next to a folder of its rows; open the CSV as a table, or build a [database view](/workspace/database-views/) over the rows |
| Toggles, callouts | Markdown lists and blockquotes |
| Comments, page history, permissions | not in the export |

## Hebrew

Notion keeps Hebrew page titles in file names; Lumen keeps them as they
are. Right-to-left paragraphs are detected per paragraph — see [Hebrew and
right-to-left](/editor/hebrew/).

pages.title: Moving from Obsidian
pages.description: Bring an Obsidian vault into Lumen — notes, attachments, links and Bases — and what changes on the way.
pages.md:
An Obsidian vault is a folder of Markdown files, and so is a Lumen vault:
nothing has to be converted.

## Bring the vault in

1. In Obsidian nothing needs exporting. Zip the vault folder, or keep it as
   a folder.
2. In Lumen: `⌘K → Import notes from another app (Obsidian, Notion, Evernote, Bear, Keep, Logseq, OneNote…)…`
   and pick the .zip or the folder.
3. Lumen recognises the vault by its `.obsidian/` folder and imports every
   note and attachment into a new folder, `Imported/<vault name>`. Nothing
   that is already in Lumen is overwritten. Obsidian's own settings
   (`.obsidian/`, `.trash/`) stay behind.

Details and the full list of what is skipped: [Export and
import](/workspace/export-import/).

## What carries over

| In Obsidian | In Lumen |
|---|---|
| `[[wikilinks]]`, `[[note#heading]]`, `![[embeds]]` | the same syntax |
| Frontmatter properties, `tags:` | the same YAML; the tags panel and database views read it |
| Attachments (images, PDFs) | the same files, the same relative links |
| Callouts `> [!note]` | shown as a quote; Lumen's callouts are `:::note` blocks |
| Canvas (`.canvas`) | kept as files |
| Plugins and themes | not carried over: Lumen has its own [plugins](/plugins/sdk/) |

## Daily habits

- **Command palette**: `⌘K`, as `⌘P` in Obsidian. [Keyboard
  shortcuts](/getting-started/shortcuts/) lists the rest.
- **Hebrew**: the editor and preview are right-to-left aware per paragraph;
  see [Hebrew and right-to-left](/editor/hebrew/).
- **Sync**: Obsidian Sync does not reach Lumen. Use Git, or keep the vault
  in a folder both apps open on the desktop.

## Going back

Your notes stay plain Markdown. `⌘K → Export the whole vault…` gives you a
.zip or a folder that Obsidian opens as a vault.

pages.title: Install with a package manager
pages.description: Install the Lumen desktop app with Homebrew, winget, Flatpak or the AUR, and where those packages come from.
pages.md:
Each release of the desktop app is published as a GitHub release. The
Homebrew cask, the winget manifests, the Flathub manifest and the AUR
package are all generated from that release's `SHA256SUMS`, so every
channel installs the same files.

| System | Command |
|---|---|
| macOS (Homebrew) | `brew install --cask lumen-md` |
| Windows (winget) | `winget install Talstilkol.Lumen` |
| Linux (Flathub) | `flatpak install flathub io.github.talstilkol.Lumen` |
| Arch Linux (AUR) | `yay -S lumen-md-bin` (or any AUR helper) |

A channel works once the owner has submitted that release to it. Until
then, download the installer from the GitHub release and check it with
`SHA256SUMS`.

## Updates

- Homebrew, winget, Flatpak and the AUR update the app like any other
  package.
- The app's own updater ([Desktop app updates](/getting-started/desktop-updates/))
  stays on, and checks the same signed release.

## The Flatpak sandbox

The Flatpak app may use the network (sync, model downloads, and cloud AI
when you allow it) and your `Documents` folder. A vault in any other
folder opens through the system's file picker, which grants access to
that folder only.

## For maintainers

`node scripts/release.mjs packages` writes every manifest and checks it
offline. See `RELEASE.md`, "Stores and package managers".

pages.title: Install Lumen
pages.description: Lumen in the browser, as an installed web app, on the desktop (macOS, Windows, Linux) and on iOS / Android — and what each one stores where.
pages.md:
Lumen is the same app on every platform. The only differences are where
your notes are kept and how the app is updated.

| Platform | How | Notes are kept in |
|---|---|---|
| Browser | open the hosted app, or `npm run dev` from a clone | the browser's private file system (OPFS) |
| Installed web app (PWA) | the browser's **Install** button on the hosted app | the same OPFS; works offline |
| macOS / Windows / Linux | build with `npm run tauri:build` (Tauri 2) | a real folder on disk |
| iOS | `npm run ios:open` (Capacitor, opens Xcode) | the app's storage |
| Android | `npm run android:open` (Capacitor, opens Android Studio) | the app's storage |

## In the browser

Nothing to install. Notes stay in this browser's private storage and never
leave the device unless you turn on sync. **Clearing the site's data
deletes them**, so export the vault (*Export the whole vault…*, see
[Export and import](/workspace/export-import/)) before you clear
browser data, or keep the vault in a real folder.

The minimum versions (set by Tailwind CSS 4) are Safari and iOS 16.4+,
Chrome / Edge 111+ and Firefox 128+.

## Installed web app (offline)

Use the browser's install button (Chrome, Edge) or *Share → Add to Home
Screen* (Safari). The installed app opens without a network: the editor,
highlighting, fonts and your files are all cached.

## Desktop

There are no signed release builds yet, so build from a clone:

```bash
npm ci
npm run tauri:build
```

The desktop app keeps the vault as a folder of plain `.md` files that
other tools (git, Obsidian, a text editor) can open, and keeps secrets in
the OS keychain on macOS and Windows (see
[How Lumen stores your secrets](/security/vault/)). On Linux it needs
WebKitGTK 2.40+.

## iOS and Android

The mobile projects are generated with Capacitor:

```bash
npm ci
npm run ios:open        # or: npm run android:open
```

Then build and run from Xcode or Android Studio.

## Running from source

```bash
git clone https://github.com/talstilkol/lumen-md
cd lumen-md
npm ci
npm run dev
```

pages.md:
## 1. Open Lumen

Either visit [lumen.app](https://lumen.app) (the hosted PWA), install the
desktop app (see [Install Lumen](/getting-started/install/)), or run
locally:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/talstilkol/lumen-md
cd lumen-md
npm ci
npm run dev
```

## 2. Type your first note

Hit `⌘N` for a fresh document. Try the smart paste — `⌘⇧V` opens an
"Insert anything…" dialog. Drop in:

- a YouTube link → it wraps as `\`\`\`embed`
- a CSV row → it wraps as `\`\`\`csv` and shows a sortable table + chart
  suggestions
- a SQL `CREATE TABLE` → ditto, parsed as data
- Mermaid `flowchart LR …` → renders as SVG
- A LaTeX equation → math typeset by KaTeX

## 3. Save it

`⌘S` saves to your local OPFS workspace. Open the workspace pane
(`⌘K → Toggle workspace`) to browse / rename / move files. Everything is
just markdown — your notes remain portable.

## 4. Power-user keys

| Key | Action |
| --- | --- |
| `⌘K` | Command palette (everything is here) |
| `⇧⌘F` | Focus mode |
| `⌘⇧V` | Smart Insert (auto-detect) |
| `⌘1`–`⌘4` | Source / Split / Preview / WYSIWYG |
| `⌘H` | Find and replace |
| `⌘O` / `⌘N` | Open / New |

Workspace search is `⌘K → Search workspace…`; the full list is on
[Keyboard shortcuts](/getting-started/shortcuts/).

Now start writing — and explore the [Editor modes](/editor/modes/) for the
heavier surfaces.

pages.description: Why we built Lumen, and what makes it different from Obsidian, Notion, Typora, Bear.
pages.md:
## Where Lumen fits

There's no shortage of markdown editors — Obsidian, Notion, Typora, Bear,
Logseq, Roam, HackMD, Joplin, Craft. Lumen sits at a specific intersection:

| | Lumen | Obsidian | Notion | Typora | Bear |
| --- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Local-first (works offline) | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Web app (no install) | ✅ | ❌ | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ |
| Auto data → table + chart | ✅ | ⚠️ plugins | ⚠️ DB only | ❌ | ❌ |
| RTL / Hebrew first-class | ✅ | ⚠️ | ⚠️ | ⚠️ | ⚠️ |
| Mermaid + Graphviz + PlantUML + ABC + 3D | ✅ | ⚠️ plugins | ⚠️ Mermaid only | ⚠️ | ❌ |
| Real-time collab | ✅ WebRTC | ❌ | ✅ Pro | ❌ | ❌ |
| Smart search (embeddings) | ✅ Pro | ⚠️ plugin | ✅ AI | ❌ | ❌ |
| MCP for AI agents | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ |
| Local LLM (WebGPU) | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ |
| Open source (MIT) | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ |

## What we believe

**1. Plain text wins.** Lumen never invents a proprietary format — every
note is portable markdown. Rendering is opinionated; storage isn't.

**2. Data is content.** A spreadsheet inside a note shouldn't need a
plugin. Drop a CSV, JSON, or SQL block and it just becomes a table with
chart suggestions.

**3. AI assists, never gates.** Bring your own key. Disable AI entirely
and Lumen still ships every other feature.

**4. Privacy is structural, not promised.** Local-first storage, transport-encrypted
(WebRTC DTLS) collab, opt-in telemetry that's off by default.

Continue to the [Quickstart](/getting-started/quickstart/) →

pages.title: What's new
pages.description: After an update, Lumen shows that version's release notes once, in your interface language.
pages.md:
When Lumen updates, the next time you open it you see **What's new**: that
version's release notes, in the language of your interface. They appear
**once per version**. A new install doesn't show them, since nothing is new
to you yet.

To read them again at any time, run `⌘K → "What's new in this version"`.

The notes ship inside the app, so they work offline.

## For maintainers: where the notes come from

- **English** is `CHANGELOG.md`, which `node scripts/release.mjs prepare`
  writes from the commit subjects (see `RELEASE.md`). Commit links and
  scopes are left out of what readers see.
- **Other languages** live in `changelog/<locale>.md`, for example
  `changelog/he.md`, with the same `## [x.y.z] - date` sections.
  `release.mjs prepare` copies each new English section into every file
  there, marked `<!-- untranslated -->`.
- To translate a release, translate the section and delete that line.
  Until then the app shows the English notes under the language's own
  headings, and says they aren't translated yet.

pages.title: Plugin API
pages.description: The lumen object a sandboxed plugin gets — every method, the capability it needs, its limits, and the UI elements.
pages.md:
A plugin's `main` is an ES module that runs in the sandbox (see
[Sandbox and permissions](/plugins/sandbox/)). It talks to Lumen only
through the global `lumen` object. Every method returns a promise. A
method whose capability you were not granted rejects with a `PluginDenied`
error.

## Events

```js
const off = lumen.on(name, (payload) => { … }); // off() unsubscribes
```

| Event | When | Payload |
|---|---|---|
| `command:<id>` | One of your commands ran | `{ source: "palette" }` |
| `render:<lang>` | A ```` ```<lang> ```` block needs rendering | `{ requestId, source }` |
| `ui:panel` / `ui:block` | A button was clicked or a field changed in your panel / block | `{ id, kind: "click" \| "change", value? }` |
| `panel:closed` | The user closed your panel | — |

Your handlers get 250 ms of CPU each time they are called. Waiting for a
`lumen.*` call does not count toward that.

## Methods

| Method | Capability | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `document.getText()` / `getFileName()` / `getSelection()` | `document:read` | `getSelection()` → `{ from, to, text }` or `null` |
| `document.setText(text)` / `insertText(text)` / `replaceSelection(text)` | `document:write` | Insert replaces the selection at the cursor |
| `vault.list(dir?)` / `vault.read(path)` | `vault:read` | Relative paths only: no `..` and no hidden folders. Reads are capped at 5 MB |
| `vault.write(path, text)` | `vault:write` | `.md`, `.txt`, `.json` or `.csv` only, 5 MB at most |
| `commands.register({ id, label, hint? }, handler?)` / `commands.unregister(id)` | `commands` | Up to 50 per plugin. The label shows "· your plugin name" |
| `panel.open({ title? })` / `panel.render(tree)` / `panel.close()` | `panel` | One plugin panel at a time |
| `renderer.register(lang)` / `renderer.result(requestId, tree)` | `renderer` | Up to 10 languages. Languages Lumen renders itself (`mermaid`, `chart`, `csv`, …) are refused |
| `settings.get()` / `settings.set(object)` | `settings` | Your own JSON, 64 KB at most |
| `storage.get(key)` / `set(key, value)` / `delete(key)` | `storage` | Your own key–value store: 1,000 keys of at most 1 MB each. Removed when you are uninstalled |
| `clipboard.writeText(text)` | `clipboard:write` | — |
| `notifications.show(text, "info" \| "success" \| "error")` | `notifications` | Shown with your name in front |
| `network.fetch(url, { method?, headers?, body? })` | `network:<origin>` | Only to the exact origin you were granted. No cookies, no redirects, 30 s timeout, 5 MB at most. Returns `{ status, headers, body }`. Recorded in the privacy ledger; blocked under local-only |
| `lumen.manifest` | — | Your manifest (read-only) |

`console.log` / `warn` / `error` are allowed, up to 120 lines a minute.

## UI elements

Panels and rendered blocks are **trees of these elements**, and nothing
else:

`text {text}` · `heading {level 1–3, text}` · `paragraph {children}` ·
`box {direction "row"|"column", gap, children}` · `list {ordered, items: [[…]]}` ·
`button {id, label, primary?, disabled?}` · `input {id, value?, placeholder?, multiline?}` ·
`checkbox {id, label, checked?}` · `select {id, value?, options: [{value, label}]}` ·
`code {text, lang?}` · `noteLink {target, label?}` (a note in the vault, never a URL) · `divider`

A tree can have at most 2,000 nodes, nest at most 24 levels deep, and hold
at most 20,000 characters of text per node. An unknown element or field is
refused.

## Examples

The examples live in `public/plugins/examples/`:

- `word-stats` — a command, a panel, settings, `document:read`
- `callout` — a code-block renderer that keeps checklist ticks in `storage`

pages.title: Developing a plugin
pages.description: Scaffold a sandboxed plugin with create-lumen-plugin, run it with hot reload in developer mode, test it in Node with the test kit, and see what it does in the Developer panel.
pages.md:
## Five minutes from nothing to a running plugin

```bash
npx create-lumen-plugin my-plugin
cd my-plugin
npm run dev        # http://127.0.0.1:5199, watches the folder
```

1. In Lumen open **Plugin gallery**, then **Developer mode** at the bottom.
   Keep `http://127.0.0.1:5199` and press **Connect**.
2. Run the command your plugin registers from `⌘K` (in the template: *My plugin*): the side panel shows the word count of the note.
3. Change `main.js` and save. Lumen reloads the plugin by itself, usually
   in well under a second. The panel shows how long the last reload took.

Nothing needs installing: the dev server and the test kit use only Node
(20 or later).

## What is in the folder

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| `lumen-plugin.json` | The manifest: id, name, version, and the capabilities the plugin asks for, each with the reason the user sees. |
| `main.js` | The plugin. It runs in the [sandbox](/plugins/sandbox/): only the `lumen` API, no DOM, no network unless asked for. |
| `test/main.test.mjs` | Tests, run with `npm test`. |
| `tools/dev-server.mjs` | The dev server behind `npm run dev`. |
| `tools/testkit.mjs` | The test kit. |

## Developer mode

Developer mode loads the plugin from the dev server instead of the
gallery:

- It connects only to this computer (`localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, `[::1]`).
- Keep the dev server on port 5199: the app's content security policy
  allows that port on this computer and no other.
- The plugin gets the capabilities its manifest asks for, without the
  permission screen: it is your own code.
- Each version is still run through the [safety scan](/plugins/permissions/),
  and the panel shows its notes. The scan's verdict does not block your own
  plugin here, but the gallery will not list a version that fails.
- On every save the dev server sends a `change` event and Lumen loads the
  manifest and `main.js` again. Changes that arrive during a reload are
  collected into one more reload.

## The Developer panel

While the plugin runs, the panel shows:

- **Reloads**: how many, how long the last one took (from the save to the
  plugin running again), and how long the start took.
- **CPU and memory**: the time spent in the plugin's code, how many runs,
  the longest, and the sandbox's memory.
- **Permissions: asked for and used**: each capability in the manifest,
  how often it was used and refused. A capability that is never used is
  marked: ask only for what you use, because users see the list before
  they install.
- **Last calls**: the plugin's last calls to Lumen, with their time and
  whether they were refused.

## Testing in Node

```js




test("shows the count", async () => {
  const p = await loadPlugin({ dir: ".", document: { text: "שלום עולם" } });
  await p.run("show");                       // a command it registered
  assert.equal(p.panel.tree.type, "box");    // the panel it rendered
});

test("needs document:read", async () => {
  const p = await loadPlugin({ dir: ".", grants: ["commands", "panel"] });
  await assert.rejects(p.run("show"), { name: "PluginDenied" });
});
```

`loadPlugin` runs `main.js` in a fresh Node `vm` context with a mock of the
`lumen` API. It follows the sandbox's rules: the same method table (a test
in Lumen keeps the two equal), a call without its capability rejects with
`PluginDenied`, and arguments must be JSON. The mock state is `document`
(`text`, `fileName`, `selection`), `vault` (`{"folder/note.md": text}`),
`settings`, `storage` and `fetch` for granted network calls.

You get back what the plugin did: `commands`, `panel`, `rendered`,
`document`, `vault`, `storage`, `notifications`, `clipboard`, `logs`,
`calls` and `denied`. You drive it with `run(id, payload)`,
`emit(name, payload)` (for example `"ui:panel"`), `render(lang, source)`
for a code-block renderer, and `select(from, to)`.

Node is not QuickJS, so test in Lumen too before you publish. Two
differences to keep in mind: QuickJS has no `Intl`, and the sandbox
limits CPU time and memory.

## Examples

The gallery's eight examples are in `public/plugins/examples/`:

| Example | Shows |
|---|---|
| Word stats | A panel, settings, Hebrew and English counting |
| Callout cards | A code-block renderer, storage |
| Quote of the day | Network access to one origin |
| Table of contents | Reading and writing the note |
| Hebrew date | A renderer and a command, a calendar computed without `Intl` |
| Tasks overview | Reading the whole vault (`vault:read`), a panel with note links |
| Bidi cleaner | Selection or whole note, notifications |
| Text format | A port of an Obsidian plugin (MIT), several commands |

## Publishing

pages.md:
A sandboxed plugin can do nothing until you allow it — see the
[plugin API](/plugins/api/). Two things make that choice informed.

## The install screen

**Plugin Gallery → Sandboxed plugins → Install…** opens a screen that lists,
before anything runs, every permission the plugin's manifest asks for:

| Permission | What it lets the plugin do |
|---|---|
| `document:read` | Read the note that is open |
| `document:write` | Change the note that is open (*sensitive*) |
| `vault:read` | Read any note in your vault (*sensitive*) |
| `vault:write` | Create and change notes in your vault (*sensitive*) |
| `commands` | Add commands to the command palette |
| `panel` | Show a side panel |
| `renderer` | Draw code blocks of its own language in the preview |
| `settings` | Keep its own settings |
| `storage` | Store its own data on this device |
| `clipboard:write` | Copy text to your clipboard (*sensitive*) |
| `notifications` | Show notifications |
| `network:<origin>` | Connect to that one address — and nowhere else (*sensitive*) |

Each line also shows the plugin's own reason (“Why: …”) and the version's
safety scan. **Install and allow** grants exactly what is listed; anything
else the plugin tries is refused by the sandbox, and every network request
appears in the privacy ledger. The code is scanned again right before it
runs, so the card can't describe a different copy.

## The safety scan

Every version in the registry (`public/plugins/examples/index.json`) is
scanned by `scripts/scan-plugins.mjs` into `scan.json`; the gallery shows
each version's card — a grade (A, B, C), a score out of 100, and what the
scan noted. **A version that fails is not shown and cannot be installed.**

The scan reads the code — it never runs it — and fails a version that:

- uses an API whose permission the manifest does not declare (for example
  writes to the note with only `document:read`);
- reaches the network without declaring it, or connects to an origin other
  than the one declared;
- runs code made from text (`eval`, `Function`, string timers), loads more
  code (`import`), or indexes `globalThis` / `lumen` with a computed key;
- is not valid JavaScript, is larger than 512 KB, or has a signature that
  does not verify.

It notes (and lowers the score for) permissions asked for but not used,
indirect use of the API, network addresses built while running, and a
missing or unknown signature.

To check a new version before publishing: add it to `index.json`, then
`node scripts/scan-plugins.mjs` (or `--check` to only verify).

## Reporting a problem

Every card and install screen has **Report a problem**, which opens an issue
with the plugin's id and version filled in.

pages.description: The ten plugins in Lumen's plugin gallery, what each one may do, and how the static registry is built and scanned.
pages.md:
The **Sandboxed plugins** section of the Plugin Gallery lists plugins from a
static registry that ships with Lumen. There is no plugin server: the registry
is a folder of files, and every version in it passes the safety scan before it
is listed.

## The ten plugins

These are modelled on the kinds of Obsidian plugins people download most
(templates, task boards, calendars, tables, linting, tags, spaced repetition,
refactoring, dates, sorting). Each is written for Lumen's sandbox: none of them
uses the network, so they all work under the **local-only** AI policy.

| Plugin | What it does | Permissions |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Templates** | Inserts a note from your `Templates` folder, filling `{{date}}`, `{{date:DD/MM/YYYY}}`, `{{time}}`, `{{title}}`, `{{selection}}`, `{{weekday}}` and `{{hebrewWeekday}}`. | commands, read the vault, read and change the open note, panel, settings |
| **Kanban board** | Draws a ` ```kanban ` block (a `## heading` per column, a `- item` per card) as columns, and copies the board as a Markdown table. | code-block renderer, commands, read and change the open note, clipboard, notifications |
| **Calendar** | A month view of your daily notes (`YYYY-MM-DD.md`). Days that have a note link to it. The week starts on Sunday, or on Monday if you choose. | commands, panel, read the vault, settings |
| **Table formatter** | Lines up the columns of every table and sorts a table by the column under the cursor. Hebrew niqqud takes no width. | commands, read and change the open note |
| **Markdown tidy** | Fixes trailing spaces, extra blank lines, heading spacing, mixed bullets and a missing final newline. It never touches code or front matter. | commands, read and change the open note, notifications, settings |
| **Tag manager** | Lists every `#tag` in the vault, Hebrew tags included, and renames a tag and its nested tags everywhere at once. | commands, panel, read and change the vault, notifications |
| **Flashcards** | Turns `question :: answer` lines into cards and schedules reviews with SM-2. The note itself is never changed. | commands, read the open note, panel, storage |
| **Note refactor** | Moves the selection into a new note and leaves a `[[link]]` in its place, or splits a note into one note per heading. | commands, read and change the open note, read and change the vault, notifications, settings |
| **Natural dates** | Turns “tomorrow”, “next Friday”, “in 3 days”, “מחר”, “יום שישי הבא” or 12/11/2026 (day first) into `[[2026-11-13]]`. | commands, read and change the open note, notifications, settings |
| **Sort lines** | Sorts the selected lines A→Z, Z→A or by length, reverses them, or removes duplicates. Sub-items stay with their item. Hebrew sorts by letter (final letters sort with their regular forms), and numbers sort by value. | commands, read and change the open note, notifications |

Install one from **Plugin Gallery → Sandboxed plugins → Install…**. The
permission screen lists everything the plugin asks for and why. Once a plugin is
installed, its card shows **Remove**, which stops the plugin and deletes the
settings and data it stored.

The plugins write their labels in English and Hebrew, because the plugin API
does not tell a plugin which language the app is in.

## How the registry is built

```
public/plugins/examples/
  index.json          ← built: every plugin, its versions, the SHA-256 of each version's code
  scan.json           ← built: the safety scan of every version
  kanban/             ← one folder per version
    lumen-plugin.json
    main.js
```

```sh
node scripts/build-plugin-registry.mjs           # rebuild index.json and scan.json
node scripts/build-plugin-registry.mjs --check   # fail if either is out of date or a version fails
```

The build does the following:

- validates every manifest;
- refuses stray files in a plugin folder (only the manifest, its entries, a `LICENSE` and a `README` are allowed);
- refuses an id and version that appear twice;
- writes `index.json`;
- scans every version (`scripts/scan-plugins.mjs`).

A new version goes in a folder of its own, for example `kanban@1.1.0`.

When you install a plugin, the app scans the downloaded code again. It refuses
the code if its SHA-256 differs from the hash in the registry scan.

## Not yet

- The plugins are **unsigned**, so their cards show the “unsigned” note.
  Signing them needs the owner's key; see [Plugin signing keys](/plugins/signing/).

pages.title: Plugin sandbox and permissions
pages.description: How Lumen runs plugins with no access by default — QuickJS for logic, UI as data, a capability list the user grants.
pages.md:
Lumen runs every plugin with **no access by default**. A plugin gets only
the capabilities you grant it when you install it, and you can revoke them
at any time.

## Where plugin code runs

| Part | Runs in | What it can reach |
|---|---|---|
| Logic (`main`) | [QuickJS](https://github.com/justjake/quickjs-emscripten) (MIT), a separate JavaScript engine compiled to WebAssembly, inside its own Web Worker | Only the `lumen` object. There is no `fetch`, `XMLHttpRequest`, `WebSocket`, `importScripts`, DOM or storage, and no `import` of other modules. |
| Interface (panels, settings, block output) | Lumen itself | The plugin sends a **tree of known elements**: text, heading, paragraph, box, list, button, input, checkbox, select, code, link to a note, divider. There is no `img`, `iframe`, `form`, `style`, `script` or HTML, and no link to a web address. |

The interface is data rather than a sandboxed iframe on purpose. CSP and the
iframe `sandbox` attribute block every channel but one: a frame may always
navigate *itself* (`location = "https://…?" + text`). A tree of known
elements has no such channel.

## Limits

Each plugin has a 32 MB heap and a 512 KB stack. It gets 250 ms of CPU each
time Lumen enters its code (an event, the reply to a call), and its console
is capped at 120 lines a minute. A plugin that goes over a limit, or throws
an error nobody catches, is stopped.

## Capabilities

| Capability | Gives |
|---|---|
| `document:read` / `document:write` | The open note's text and selection / changing it |
| `vault:read` / `vault:write` | Listing and reading notes / writing notes |
| `commands` | Commands in the palette |
| `panel` | A side panel |
| `renderer` | Rendering a code-block language |
| `settings` | A settings section |
| `storage` | Its own key–value storage |
| `clipboard:write` | Copying text |
| `notifications` | Toasts |
| `network:https://exact.origin` | Requests to **that origin only** — https (http only for localhost), no cookies, no redirects, at most 5 MB of response |

Every capability the manifest asks for comes with a reason, which is shown
to you before you grant it. A call without its capability fails inside the
plugin with `PluginDenied` and never reaches Lumen. Lumen checks the grant
a second time on the host side, because the worker is a boundary, not the
policy.

## Network and privacy

Every request a plugin makes appears in the **privacy ledger** under
"Plugin". Under the **local-only** AI policy, plugin requests are blocked
and logged as blocked, even when the plugin has a network grant.

## Manifest (`lumen-plugin.json`)

```json
{
  "schema": 1,
  "id": "org.example.word-stats",
  "name": "Word stats",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "description": "Counts words in the open note",
  "author": "Example",
  "license": "MIT",
  "main": "main.js",
  "capabilities": [
    { "id": "document:read", "reason": "To count the words of the open note" },
    { "id": "commands", "reason": "Adds the “Word stats” command" }
  ]
}
```

pages.title: Plugin signing keys
pages.description: Decide which publishers' plugins Lumen trusts.
pages.md:
Registry plugins can be signed with an **Ed25519** key. Before installing,
Lumen verifies the signature against the keys you trust, so a compromised
CDN cannot ship modified code.

## Manage trusted keys

Command palette → **Trusted plugin signing keys…**

- **Built-in** keys come from the deployment (`VITE_PLUGIN_TRUSTED_KEYS`)
  and cannot be removed from the UI.
- **Your keys** are stored in this browser. Paste the publisher's public key
  and press **Trust key**.

Each key is identified by its **fingerprint** — the SHA-256 of the public
key, in hex. Compare it with the fingerprint the publisher lists on their
website before trusting it.

## Accepted formats

- Base64 SPKI (44 bytes for Ed25519, starts with `MCow`).
- PEM: `-----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY----- … -----END PUBLIC KEY-----`.

Generate a key pair with OpenSSL:

```bash
openssl genpkey -algorithm ed25519 -out plugin-signing.pem
openssl pkey -in plugin-signing.pem -pubout
```

## Errors

pages.description: Start a note from a template — the built-in ones, the gallery, and the ones you install — and where an installed template lives.
pages.md:
## Start from a template

The command palette lists templates as commands. Pick one and it opens
as a **new, unsaved tab**: it never writes into the note you have open,
and a name that is already taken gets a number (*Meeting notes 2.md*).

## The template gallery

`⌘K → Browse template gallery` opens the gallery: filter by category,
search by name, and **Install** a template. Installing writes it to
`templates/<id>.md` in your vault and adds it to the palette under
**Templates: <name>**. It is an ordinary note, so you can edit it like
any other. With the interface in Hebrew, templates that have a Hebrew
version install in Hebrew.

The gallery's list ships with the app (`public/templates/registry.json`),
so browsing it makes no request to any other site.

## Adding a template to the gallery

See `public/templates/CONTRIBUTING.md` in the repository: one Markdown
file plus an entry in `registry.json` (and a Hebrew file under
`public/templates/he/` when there is one).
---
title: Templates and sample vaults
description: The template gallery, the twenty Israeli templates with their Bases views, placeholders, importing a template from a file, and the three sample vaults.
---

**⌘K → Browse template gallery** opens the gallery. **Install** copies a
template into your workspace as `templates/<id>.md`; from then on it is in
**⌘K → Templates**, and choosing it opens a new, unsaved note from it. The
gallery speaks the UI's language: in Hebrew you get the Hebrew name,
description and body of every template that has one.

## Templates for Israeli use cases

Twenty templates, each in Hebrew and in English:

| Area | Templates |
|---|---|
| Journal | Daily journal (with the Hebrew date), weekly review (Sunday–Thursday) |
| Student | University course (semester, credits), exam (Moed A / B), lecture summary, seminar paper |
| Research | Article to read, research log / experiment |
| Work | Team meeting, one-on-one, project (kanban), task |
| Home | Recipe (meat / dairy / pareve, Shabbat), holiday plan, apartment hunting (₪ rent, arnona, va'ad bayit) |
| Reading and writing | Book I'm reading, book chapter, character |
| Personal | Reserve duty (miluim) log, job application (kanban) |

Every one of them stores its facts as **properties** in the frontmatter, with
English keys (`type`, `status`, `due`…) and values in your language, so the
same note works in Lumen and in Obsidian.

### A Bases view with every template

Each template comes with a companion [`.base` file](/workspace/obsidian-bases/).
Installing the template also writes it to `Bases/` (for example
`Bases/Courses.base`, or `Bases/קורסים.base` in Hebrew): a table, cards or
kanban view of every note with that template's `type`, with column names in
your language. If the file is already there, it is left alone, so your
changes to the view survive a reinstall.

## Placeholders

When a template becomes a note, these are filled in — the same names as
Obsidian's core Templates plugin:

| Placeholder | Becomes |
|---|---|
| `{{title}}` | the note's name |
| `{{date}}` | today, `YYYY-MM-DD` |
| `{{time}}` | now, `HH:mm` |
| `{{hebrewDate}}` | today in the Hebrew calendar, for example `30 Heshvan 5787` |

Anything else in double braces is left as it is.

## Import a template from a file

**⌘K → Import template from file…**, or **Import from file…** at the top of
the gallery, copies a Markdown file you pick into `templates/`. A name that
is taken gets a number (`Recipe.md`, then `Recipe 2.md`), and characters that
can't be in a file name are replaced with spaces. The template is in
**⌘K → Templates** straight away.

## Sample vaults

Three ready-made vaults show the templates, links and Bases views working
together. Each opens from the command palette, in the UI's language, into a
folder of its own:

- **Open sample vault: student** — two courses, lecture summaries and an
  exam with a study plan; views of courses, lectures and exams.
- **Open sample vault: researcher** — a thesis, three articles and two
  experiments; views of the literature, the research log and the papers.
- **Open sample vault: writer** — three chapters and three characters,
  linked to each other; views of the manuscript and the characters.

Like the sample workspace, a sample vault never overwrites anything: running
it again only adds the files that are missing.

pages.description: Clip a page, a selection or your highlights into the vault as Markdown, with its source and date. No server involved.
pages.md:
The Lumen Web Clipper is a Chrome / Edge extension (Manifest V3). It sends
the page to Lumen, and **Lumen** turns it into a note. The extraction
happens in the app, so a clip comes out the same whichever way it arrives.

## Install (developer mode)

1. `chrome://extensions/` → turn on **Developer mode**
2. **Load unpacked** → pick the `extension/` folder of the repository
3. Open the extension's **Settings**: set the address of your Lumen (default
   `http://localhost:5173`), or choose **The Lumen desktop app**.

## Use

- **Save full page**: the toolbar button, or right-click → **Clip to Lumen**.
- **Save selection only**: select text first. Only the selection becomes the note.
- **Highlighter**: toolbar → **Highlighter on/off**, then select passages on
  the page. They are kept per address, marked again when you come back,
  and put at the top of the note (as `==highlight==` quotes) on the next clip.

## How a clip reaches Lumen

| Where Lumen runs | How |
|---|---|
| Browser tab | The extension finds (or opens) the Lumen tab and hands the clip to the page with `postMessage`. The app takes messages only from its own window and origin. |
| Desktop app | A `lumen://clip?…` link. If Lumen is already open, the running window gets it. |

Nothing is uploaded anywhere: there is no clip server.

## What a clip contains

The readable part of the page, found by [Defuddle](https://github.com/kepano/defuddle)
(MIT), with Mozilla Readability (Apache-2.0) as a fallback, and converted to
Markdown by Turndown (MIT):

```yaml
---
title: "The Counterpane"
source: "https://example.com/story"
author: "Ada Pierce"
published: "2026-10-01"
clipped: "2026-10-24"
tags: [clip]
---
```

Links and images point at the original page. Clips go into the library
folder (`Library/`, or `ספרייה/` when Lumen is in Hebrew).

### Templates by site

| Site | Folder | Extra |
|---|---|---|
| Wikipedia (any language) | `Library/Wikipedia` | `license: CC BY-SA 4.0`, `summary` |
| ynet | `Library/ynet` | `summary`, `topics`, `tags: [clip, news]` |
| Haaretz | `Library/Haaretz` | `summary`, `topics`, `tags: [clip, news]` |
| YouTube | `Library/YouTube` | `channel`, `published`, `summary`; the transcript when its panel is open |
| arXiv | `Library/arXiv` | `authors`, `arxiv`, `published`, `pdf`, `contribution`; the abstract |
| GitHub repositories | `Library/GitHub` | `description`, `purpose` |
| Pages marked as a schema.org `Recipe` | `Library/Recipes` | `tags: [clip, recipe]` |

A template is picked by its triggers: an address prefix, a `/regular expression/`
or `schema:@Type`. The first match wins.

Besides `{{title}}`, `{{url}}`, `{{content}}` and the rest, a template can read
the page with `{{meta:name}}` (a `<meta>` tag, by name, property or itemprop;
several tags of one name are joined) and `{{selector:css}}` (the text of the
elements a CSS selector picks).

## Interpreter: fields a local model fills in

A template can ask questions about the page: `{{"a one-sentence summary"}}`,
`{{"three key topics"|lower}}`. When a clip uses such a template, Lumen asks a
**model on your own device** — Ollama on this computer or your local network,
or the in-browser model if it is already loaded — and writes the answers into
the note. There is no cloud route: under any AI policy, the interpreter never
sends a page to an AI provider. With no local model running, those fields are
left out and the clip is saved as usual.

- The model reads only what the template points at (its `context` selectors:
  the abstract on arXiv, the lead section on Wikipedia, the transcript on
  YouTube), cut to about 6 000 characters, so a small model's window is
  enough. No `OLLAMA_ORIGINS` or context-size setting is needed in the
  desktop app.
- All questions of a template go in one request.
- The page text passes the prompt-injection guard before the model sees it,
  marked as outside data, and every answer is checked again before it is
  written into the note.

## Safety

A clip is outside content. Its `source:` marks the note as untrusted for the
AI agents (plan 2.7). Before the
note is saved, hidden text (zero-width characters, invisible tag characters,
hidden HTML) and instruction-like passages ("ignore previous instructions…")
are removed or visibly marked, with a warning at the top of the note.

## Accuracy

On the clipper golden set (plan 7.10: 20 pages with ads, cookie banners,
share bars, comments and footers around a public-domain article), the clip
must have the exact title, every paragraph in order and no noise on at least
90 % of pages. This is checked on every change (`clipperGolden.test.ts`).

pages.description: Where to talk about Lumen, how the Hebrew beta works, how to join, and the code of conduct.
pages.md:
Lumen is built in the open, in Hebrew and English.

## The beta

- **Joining:** open a discussion in the **Beta** category of the project's
  GitHub Discussions. It's a short form, and you need a GitHub account.
  The beta page (`/beta.html`) explains it all and sends nothing by itself.
- **What you get:** new features before everyone else. They ship behind
  feature flags in beta builds first.
- **What we ask:** use Lumen for real writing a few times a week, and tell
  us what got in the way, in **Beta feedback**.
- **The weekly survey:** a short, voluntary poll, *how many days this week
  did you open Lumen?* It is the only way we count testers. Lumen has no
  analytics and doesn't count you.
- **Keep a backup:** *Export the whole vault* now and then. It's a beta.

## Where to talk

| For | Where |
|---|---|
| Beta feedback: bugs, ideas, Hebrew and RTL problems | Discussions → *Beta feedback* |
| A confirmed bug or a concrete feature | GitHub Issues |
| Questions, show and tell | Discussions → *Q&A*, *Show and tell* |
| Security problems | privately, as in `SECURITY.md` |

Hebrew or English, whichever you prefer.

## The code of conduct

The project follows the
[Contributor Covenant 2.1](https://www.contributor-covenant.org/version/2/1/code_of_conduct.html).
The repository has it in English (`CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md`) and in Hebrew
(`CODE_OF_CONDUCT.he.md`). In short:

- assume good intent;
- criticise the work, not the person;
- no harassment, no personal attacks, no sharing others' private
  information.

Reports go privately to the maintainers, as described in `COMMUNITY.md`,
and are kept confidential.

## How Lumen compares

The [comparison page](/project/compare/) puts Lumen next to Obsidian, Notion
and Google Docs on five points, with a source for every claim and a list of
what Lumen still lacks.

pages.title: Lumen, Obsidian, Notion and Google Docs
pages.description: An honest comparison for people who write in Hebrew: what each one does, with a source for every claim, and what Lumen still lacks.
pages.md:
Each one is good at something. This page says what each does on five points that matter when you write in Hebrew, and every claim links to where it can be checked. Claims about the other products come from their own pages.

## Price

| | What it does | Sources |
|---|---|---|
| **Lumen** | Free. In the browser there is nothing to install, and notes stay in the browser's private storage. | [Lumen docs](/getting-started/install/) · <https://github.com/talstilkol/lumen-md/blob/main/LICENSE> (Checked 2026-11-10) |
| **Obsidian** | Free, for personal use and, since February 2025, for work too. Sync is a paid add-on ($4 a month, billed yearly). | <https://obsidian.md/blog/free-for-work/> · <https://obsidian.md/pricing.html> (Checked 2026-11-10) |
| **Notion** | A free plan and paid plans; see Notion's pricing page. | <https://www.notion.com/pricing> (⚠ not yet verified) |
| **Google Docs** | Free with a Google account; Google Workspace plans for organisations. | <https://workspace.google.com/pricing> (⚠ not yet verified) |

## Hebrew and right-to-left

| | What it does | Sources |
|---|---|---|
| **Lumen** | Interface in Hebrew with a mirrored layout; direction per line; search that ignores niqqud and Hebrew prefixes. | [Lumen docs](/editor/hebrew/) (Checked 2026-11-10) |
| **Obsidian** | Since version 1.6: a mirrored interface for right-to-left languages, Hebrew among them, and notes in RTL, LTR or both. | <https://docs.obsidian.md/Plugins/User+interface/Right-to-left> (Checked 2026-11-10) |
| **Notion** | Interface in Hebrew, mirrored in the desktop and mobile apps; text direction detected in most blocks, but not in simple tables. | <https://www.notion.com/help/change-your-language> (Checked 2026-11-10) |
| **Google Docs** | Right-to-left controls turn on for documents with RTL text; paragraph direction and table column order can be set. | <https://support.google.com/docs/answer/65166> (Checked 2026-11-10) |

## Working offline

| | What it does | Sources |
|---|---|---|
| **Lumen** | The installed web app opens and works without a network; notes are stored on the device. | [Lumen docs](/getting-started/install/) (Checked 2026-11-10) |
| **Obsidian** | Notes are files in a folder on the device, so they open without a network. | <https://help.obsidian.md/data-storage> (⚠ not yet verified) |
| **Notion** | Since August 2025, offline in the desktop and mobile apps (not the browser): downloaded pages, plus Recents and Favorites on Plus, Business and Enterprise. | <https://www.notion.com/releases/2025-08-19> (Checked 2026-11-10) |
| **Google Docs** | Offline editing in Chrome or Edge with the Google Docs Offline extension, turned on per account. | <https://support.google.com/docs/answer/6388102> (⚠ not yet verified) |

## Markdown files

| | What it does | Sources |
|---|---|---|
| **Lumen** | Every note is a plain Markdown file; the whole vault exports as a .zip or a folder. | [Lumen docs](/workspace/export-import/) (Checked 2026-11-10) |
| **Obsidian** | Notes are Markdown files. | <https://help.obsidian.md/data-storage> (⚠ not yet verified) |
| **Notion** | Pages live in Notion's database; they can be exported as Markdown. | <https://www.notion.com/help/export-your-content> (⚠ not yet verified) |
| **Google Docs** | Since July 2024, import Markdown as a Doc and export a Doc as Markdown. | <https://workspaceupdates.googleblog.com/2024/07/import-and-export-markdown-in-google-docs.html> (Checked 2026-11-10) |

## Source code

| | What it does | Sources |
|---|---|---|
| **Lumen** | Open source under the MIT licence. | <https://github.com/talstilkol/lumen-md/blob/main/LICENSE> (Checked 2026-11-10) |
| **Obsidian** | The app's source code is not published. | <https://obsidian.md/license> (⚠ not yet verified) |
| **Notion** | Proprietary. | <https://www.notion.com/terms> (⚠ not yet verified) |
| **Google Docs** | Proprietary. | <https://policies.google.com/terms> (⚠ not yet verified) |

## What Lumen still lacks

- No sync service of its own yet: between devices, keep the vault in a folder you already sync, or export and import. ([Lumen docs](/workspace/export-import/))
- Real-time co-editing is peer to peer and young; Google Docs and Notion are far ahead for teams. ([Lumen docs](/collab/webrtc/))
- Far fewer plugins and templates than Obsidian's community. ([Lumen docs](/plugins/sdk/))
- The phone apps are not in the App Store or Google Play yet; on a phone Lumen runs in the browser or as an installed web app. ([Lumen docs](/getting-started/install/))
- It is a beta: expect rough edges, and keep a backup (Export the whole vault). ([Lumen docs](/workspace/export-import/))

This page is generated from `launch/comparison.json` by `node scripts/launch-check.mjs --write`. To correct a claim, change the JSON with a source, and the page follows.

pages.title: Issue triage
pages.description: How new GitHub issues are labelled, checked for duplicates and linked to the plan within 24 hours.
pages.md:
Every new issue on [talstilkol/lumen-md](https://github.com/talstilkol/lumen-md/issues)
is looked at by a script within 24 hours, and a person reads it as well. The
script is `scripts/issue-triage.mjs`; the workflow `.github/workflows/issue-triage.yml`
runs it when an issue is opened or reopened and once a day at 06:23 UTC.

## What an issue gets

| What | When | Label |
|---|---|---|
| Kind | from words in the title and body (English and Hebrew) | `bug`, `enhancement`, `question` or `documentation` |
| Area | up to two, the ones whose words appear most | `area:editor`, `area:hebrew`, `area:ai`, `area:storage`, … |
| Possible duplicate | another issue, open or closed, has a near-identical title | `duplicate?` |
| Reproduction request | a bug with no steps, browser or version | `needs-repro` |
| Plan task | a task number in the text (for example `4.5`), else the plan task whose title shares the most words | — (in the comment) |
| Done | always | `triaged` |

When there is something to say (a possible duplicate, missing steps, a plan
task) the script leaves **one** comment, in English and Hebrew. It finds its
own comment again by a hidden marker, so a rerun never comments twice. Labels
that do not exist yet are created.

## What it does not do

- It never closes, assigns or edits an issue, and never removes a label.
- Issue text is only matched against word lists: it is not executed and not
  sent anywhere. The script talks to GitHub's REST API through `gh` with the
  workflow's own token (`issues: write`) and nothing else.

## The daily report

The daily run writes a report — the issues of the last 24 hours with the labels,
duplicate and plan task each got — to the job summary and as the artifact
`reports-issue-triage`. Any open issue older than 24 hours that still has no
`triaged` label is listed and **fails the run**, so the 24-hour promise is
checked every day.

## Running it yourself

```bash
node scripts/issue-triage.mjs                 # dry run: prints what it would do
node scripts/issue-triage.mjs --apply         # writes labels and comments
node scripts/issue-triage.mjs --json out.json # the report as JSON too
```

A dry run needs only a logged-in `gh`; `--apply` needs write access to issues.

pages.title: Releasing a version
pages.description: One local command builds, signs and checks a release, and with --publish puts it on GitHub Releases with signed desktop updates. No GitHub Actions.
pages.md:
A release is one command on the release owner's computer. GitHub Actions
are not needed.

```bash
npm run release -- 0.2.0-beta.1 --dry-run     # build, sign and check everything; publish nothing
npm run release -- 0.2.0-beta.1 --publish     # the owner: commit, tag, build, sign, push, GitHub release
```

A dry run puts the tree back when it finishes: the version, `CHANGELOG.md` and
`src-tauri/tauri.conf.json` return to what they were. It leaves `release/`
with every asset, plus `release/DRY-RUN.md`, which lists the assets and the
exact commands `--publish` would run.

## What the command does

1. **Preflight.** It lists everything that is missing (a key, a tool, the
   release notes, a clean tree, the `main` branch, `gh auth`), each with the
   command that fixes it. A dry run needs no key. A publish needs every one.
2. **Version and changelog.** It bumps the version in `package.json`,
   `package-lock.json`, `tauri.conf.json`, `Cargo.toml` and the iOS project.
   It writes the `CHANGELOG.md` section from the pull requests merged since
   the last tag: one line per PR, sorted by the type in its title (Added,
   Fixed, Performance, …), with a link to the PR. PR titles come from the
   GitHub API; offline (`--offline`) it uses the merge commits.
3. **Commit and tag** (`--publish` only): `chore(release): X` and `vX`.
4. **The updater.** The committed `tauri.conf.json` carries the placeholder
   `${LUMEN_UPDATER_PUBKEY}`. The release fills in the public key and the
   endpoint on GitHub Releases (stable: `releases/latest/download/latest.json`;
   a beta: the rolling `beta-channel` release). It also turns on signed update
   bundles. The build stops if the key is empty, is still the placeholder or
   is not a minisign key. Afterwards the file goes back to the placeholder.
5. **A reproducible web build.** `repro-check` builds twice with
   `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` and compares every file, then the bundle budget and the
   source-map check run. `lumen-web-vX.tgz` is the same bytes on every machine:
   the files are sorted, the owner and mode are fixed, and the gzip header has
   no time.
6. **Desktop.** `tauri build` runs with `TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY`. The macOS
   update bundle gets its version and architecture in its name.
   `latest.json` is built from the `.sig` files. Every signature is checked
   against the updater key, and the same check must refuse a copy with one
   byte changed.
7. **SBOM.** `sbom.cdx.json` (CycloneDX 1.5) lists every package in
   `package-lock.json` and every crate in `Cargo.lock`. It is built offline.
8. **Release notes.** Hebrew first, then English, from
   `release-notes/<version>.he.md` and `release-notes/<version>.en.md`
   (written by hand, a few lines each), then the full change list and how to
   verify the download.
9. **Checksums.** `SHA256SUMS` lists every asset. It is signed with minisign
   (`SHA256SUMS.minisig`), and so is the SBOM. The whole folder is then
   verified, and a changed `SHA256SUMS` must fail.
10. **Publish** (`--publish` only): `git push origin HEAD vX`, then
    `gh release create`. A beta is a pre-release and is never "latest", so
    stable users never get it. Then `latest.json` is uploaded to the
    `beta-channel` release.

## Options

| Option | What it does |
|---|---|
| `--dry-run` | the default: nothing is committed, tagged or published |
| `--publish` | the real release (the owner) |
| `--fake-build` | dry run only: stand-in bundles where `node_modules`, Rust or the Tauri CLI are missing; every later step still runs. A publish refuses it. |
| `--no-repro` | one web build instead of two |
| `--no-desktop` | web, SBOM and checksums only |
| `--skip-checks` | no typecheck and no tests before the build |
| `--offline` | PR titles from git, not from the GitHub API |

## Keys (made once, kept by the owner)

| Key | Made with | Used through |
|---|---|---|
| Updater signing key | `npx tauri signer generate -w ~/.tauri/lumen-updater.key` | `TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY` (+ `TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD`) |
| Updater public key | written next to it (`.key.pub`) | commit it as `security/updater-key.pub`, or set `LUMEN_UPDATER_PUBKEY` |
| Release key (checksums, SBOM) | `node scripts/supply-chain/keys.mjs` | `LUMEN_RELEASE_KEY` (+ `LUMEN_RELEASE_PASSPHRASE`); commit `security/release-key.pub` |

When a key is missing, a dry run signs with throwaway test keys and says so.
Their public keys have `TEST` in their comment line, and a publish refuses
them.

## Checking a release (anyone)

```bash
gh release download v0.2.0-beta.1 --repo talstilkol/lumen-md --dir lumen
cd lumen && minisign -Vm SHA256SUMS -p release-key.pub && sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS
# or, without minisign:
node scripts/supply-chain/verify-release.mjs lumen --pub security/release-key.pub
```

## Limits

- One `--publish` run uploads the bundles of the machine it runs on: the
  macOS bundles from a Mac. Bundles for Linux and Windows from other
  machines are not added to the same release yet. Until they are, publish
  from the Mac (that gives at least the `.dmg`, the update bundle, its
  signature, the web `.tgz` and the SBOM).
- Rolling back is `node scripts/release.mjs rollback <bad> --to <good>` (see
  `RELEASE.md`).

pages.title: Public roadmap
pages.description: The roadmap page at /roadmap — generated from plan/plan.json, titles and status only, and checked in CI so it cannot drift.
pages.md:
Every Lumen deployment serves an open roadmap at `/roadmap.html` (and at
`/roadmap` on Cloudflare Pages, Netlify and the Docker image). The status bar's
**Roadmap** link opens it.

## Where it comes from

The page is the third output of `npm run plan`, next to the board in
`MASTER_PLAN.md` and `plan/board.html`. All three are rendered from one file,
`plan/plan.json`, and `npm run plan:check` fails CI when any of them differs
from it. So the roadmap changes in the same commit as the plan, every time.

## What it shows — and what it does not

| Shown | Not shown |
|---|---|
| every phase, with its number and title | the steps of a task and its acceptance line |
| every task's number and title | estimates, dates and the schedule |
| its state: **done** (✅), **in progress** (⏳) or **planned** | branches, PR numbers and the owner's items (phase 15) |
| the counts and a progress bar | anything from issues or notes |

The full plan, with every measured acceptance criterion, is in the repository.

## How it renders

`public/roadmap.html` carries the data as a JSON block; `public/roadmap.js`
builds the cards with `textContent`. The script is external because the app's
Content-Security-Policy allows no inline script, and it needs no Trusted Types
policy because it never writes HTML. The page is Hebrew and right-to-left,
laid out with logical CSS properties.

## Updating it

```bash
npm run plan        # rewrites MASTER_PLAN.md's board, plan/board.html and public/roadmap.html
npm run plan:check  # what CI runs: exit 1 when any of them is out of date
```

pages.title: Sustainability
pages.description: How Lumen pays for itself without ads, accounts or locked features. Donations through GitHub Sponsors and Open Collective, an optional paid relay that sees only ciphertext, and every cost in the open.
pages.md:
Lumen is open source and mostly built by one person. This page is the plan for keeping it running. The live, script-free summary is the [support page](https://lumen-md.vercel.app/support.html).

## Principles

- **Every feature stays free and local.** Nothing in the app is locked behind a payment.
- **Money pays for hosting only.** The one paid product is an optional managed sync relay. Running your own relay stays free (`node sync-server/vault-relay.js`, from sync in two clicks, #483).
- **The paid relay sees no content,** the same as the free one. Notes are encrypted on the device before they leave it ([encrypted sync](/sync/e2ee/)).
- **Every cost is public.** The support page lists what Lumen pays each month, and `scripts/cost-model.mjs` computes the paid tier's numbers. A test checks that the page and the model agree.

## What it costs today

| Service | What for | Per month |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Vercel Hobby | The app at lumen-md.vercel.app | $0 |
| Cloudflare Workers, free plan | The [public live-share server](/collab/public-server/) | $0 |
| GitHub | Code, issues, releases | $0 |

**Total: $0.** Vercel's Hobby plan is for non-commercial use only. Asking for donations is allowed, but selling anything, the relay included, is commercial use under [Vercel's fair-use guidelines](https://vercel.com/docs/limits/fair-use-guidelines). Before the paid relay launches, the app moves to a host that allows commercial use, or to Vercel Pro (plan W4.27).

## Donations

| Channel | Fee | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [GitHub Sponsors](https://docs.github.com/en/sponsors/getting-started-with-github-sponsors/about-github-sponsors), personal account | 0% from personal sponsors. Organizations pay up to 6% (3% card processing and 3% service). | No fee, and Israel is a supported region for receiving money. |
| [Open Collective](https://opencollective.com) through [Open Source Collective](https://opencollective.com/opensource/apply/intro) | 10% host fee, plus the card processor's fee | A public ledger: every donation and every expense, with receipts. |

### Choosing a fiscal host (researched 12.11.2026)

A fiscal host holds the money, keeps the books and pays expenses for a collective that has no legal entity of its own.

| Host | Fit for Lumen | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Open Source Collective** | **Chosen** | Hosts open-source projects. Host fee 10% ([application page](https://opencollective.com/opensource/apply/intro)). Verification through GitHub, or manual review. |
| Open Collective Europe | No | For projects rooted in or connected to Europe ([Open Collective's list of hosting options](https://blog.opencollective.com/fiscal-hosting-options)). |
| Open Collective Foundation | No | Dissolved on 31.12.2024 ([announcement](https://blog.opencollective.com/open-collective-official-statement-ocf-dissolution/)). |
| Huddlecraft | No | UK-based projects or projects in GBP. 4.25% plus a £50 setup fee. |
| The Social Change Nest | Possible | A UK CIC that can host groups outside the UK. It hosts social causes, not specifically software. |

Payouts from Open Source Collective reach an Israeli bank account through Wise or PayPal. Their fees depend on the currency and the country ([payment processor fees](https://documentation.opencollective.com/expenses-and-getting-paid/payment-processor-fees)).

## The paid relay (optional, planned)

### What it is

The same blob protocol as the relay of sync in two clicks (`sync-server/vault-relay.js`, #483), run by Lumen for people who don't want to run their own. The app talks to it exactly as it talks to a self-hosted relay. The only difference is `VITE_SYNC_RELAY_URL`. There are no accounts in the app.

### Where it runs

On the Cloudflare account that already runs the public live-share server (#469, `edge-workers/collab/`), as a second Worker:

- **R2** holds the objects. Each key is the SHA-256 of the space plus the object name, which is already an HMAC chosen by the app.
- **One Durable Object per space** makes `If-Match` / `If-None-Match` writes atomic and keeps the object list, the ETags and the byte count in its SQLite storage. The relay's store interface (`createVaultRelay({ store })`) is the seam: an R2 store plus a per-space Durable Object lock implement the same `list / get / put / delete / bytes / sweep` methods that the tests already check.
- Limits: 10 GB per paid space, 25 MiB per object, and the same rate limit as the Node relay. Request logging stays off, as for #469.

### What it sees

| | The paid relay |
| --- | --- |
| Note text, titles, file names | **Never.** The device encrypts everything, and object names are HMACs. |
| Your key or recovery words | **Never.** The space is named by a token derived from the words (#483). The relay keeps only the token's SHA-256. |
| Sizes and times of encrypted objects | Yes |
| Who paid | No. That stays with the payment provider. The relay keeps only a keyed hash of the licence, tied to one space (see below). |

### Paying without an account

1. Phase 1: a **licence key** from the merchant of record (Polar issues licence keys with each purchase). The app sends it once, together with the space token. The Worker checks it against the provider's API and stores `HMAC(secret, licence id) → (space hash, plan, expiry)`. The provider knows who paid but never learns the space. The relay knows the space but not who paid. The two can be linked only by combining both records.
2. Phase 2: **unlinkable tokens**, with blind signatures (RSA blind signatures, RFC 9474, as used in Privacy Pass). The payment issues blinded tokens and the relay redeems them, so not even the combined records connect a payer to a space.
3. When a subscription ends, the space becomes read-only for 30 days and is deleted after 90 days. Every device still has the notes. Free self-hosting stays one command away.

## Cost per user and break-even

From `node scripts/cost-model.mjs`, with list prices checked on 12.11.2026: [Workers](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/pricing/), [Durable Objects](https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/platform/pricing/), [R2](https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/pricing/) and [Polar](https://polar.sh/docs/fees). The usage assumption is an active note-taker with 2–3 devices: 1 GB encrypted, about 100 writes and 1,000 reads a day.

| Per paying user per month | USD |
| --- | --- |
| R2 storage (1 GB) | $0.0150 |
| R2 writes (3,000) | $0.0135 |
| R2 reads (30,000) | $0.0108 |
| Worker requests | $0.0099 |
| Durable Object requests | $0.0005 |
| **Infrastructure total** | **$0.0496** |

| | Monthly plan, $3 | Yearly plan, $30 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Payment fee per payment (Polar Starter, 5% + $0.50, +1.5% for a non-US card) | $0.6950 | $2.45 |
| Left per subscriber per month | $2.26 | $2.25 |

| Fixed per month | USD | Break-even |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Workers Paid ($5) + a domain (about $10.44 a year), app on a free host | $5.87 | **3 subscribers** |
| The same, app on Vercel Pro ($20) | $25.87 | **12 subscribers** |

The model does not count the owner's time or an accountant's fee. Those depend on the owner's choices (see below). Storage dominates only for very large vaults: at the 10 GB cap, a user costs about $0.18 a month.

## Taking payments

| Option | For an Israeli seller | Verdict |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Polar** (merchant of record) | Pays out to Israel through Stripe Connect Express ([supported countries](https://polar.sh/docs/merchant-of-record/supported-countries)). Starter: 5% + $0.50, +1.5% for cards outside the US. Licence keys built in. Its code is open source. | **Chosen** |
| Paddle (merchant of record) | 5% + $0.50. Mature, aimed at software companies, with a review before selling. | Fallback |
| Lemon Squeezy (merchant of record) | 5% + $0.50. Now owned by Stripe and moving to Stripe Managed Payments, which supports merchants in 35+ countries ([2026 update](https://www.lemonsqueezy.com/blog/2026-update)). Israel is not confirmed. | Not now |

7. **Privacy policy and terms.** Update the privacy policy (#456) for what the provider and the relay keep, and add short terms for the paid relay.
8. **Every month.** Update the support page's cost table and the cost model's prices from the real invoices, and post the same numbers on Open Collective.

pages.title: Usability tests with Hebrew speakers
pages.description: How Lumen is tested with people who write in Hebrew — the ten tasks, SUS, the consent-first session recorder that keeps no note text, and the analysis.
pages.md:
The project measures a lot, and sessions with real people measure what
nothing else does: whether someone who writes in Hebrew can do the common
things without help. The kit is in
[`research/usability/`](https://github.com/talstilkol/lumen-md/tree/main/research/usability)
and everything in it is in Hebrew, the participants' language.

## The study

- **Who:** 8 participants per round, at least 5: two students, two
  researchers, two writers and two developers. All work in Hebrew and are new
  to Lumen.
- **What:** ten tasks, one at a time, thinking aloud, with no help from the
  moderator:
  1. a new note;
  2. a checklist;
  3. linking notes;
  4. search;
  5. tags;
  6. Hebrew and English on one line;
  7. a table;
  8. export to PDF;
  9. restoring from the trash;
  10. the daily note.
- **Measured:**
  - success, success without help, and time, per task;
  - the ease question (SEQ, 1–7) after each task;
  - the System Usability Scale (SUS, 0–100) at the end.
- **Rounds:** the ten most severe issues from round 1 become plan tasks.
  Round 2, with new participants, checks the fixes. The goal is a mean SUS
  of at least 80, at least 90% unaided success, and all ten severe issues
  closed. The study is repeated before every major release.

## Take the test on your own

You can help without a meeting. The session takes about 30 minutes, on your own.

1. Open lumen-md.vercel.app in a **private window**.
2. Open the command palette (Ctrl+K, or ⌘K on a Mac) and choose **Usability test (self-guided)…**.
3. Read what is recorded and agree.

What happens then:

- Lumen gives you a random code such as `U-7K3F`, never your name.
- It adds a few practice notes to a folder named `בדיקת שימושיות`.
- It shows ten short tasks one at a time. You press **Done** or **I couldn't do it**, then rate how easy the task was.
- At the end come ten short statements about Lumen.

Where a task's result can be seen in the practice notes, Lumen checks it on
your device and keeps only **yes or no**, never the text.

At the end you save one `.zip` file and send it through the link in your
invitation. Then press **Delete my session data**. Nothing is sent until you
send the file yourself.

## The session recorder

Command palette → **Usability study (moderator)…** opens the moderator's
panel. It is off until then, and it records nothing until the participant
has signed the consent form and the moderator ticks the box.

| Recorded | Never recorded |
|---|---|
| when each task started and ended, and its outcome | anything typed into notes, note or file names |
| controls clicked, by role and by the app's own label | a label that isn't one of the app's UI strings (it becomes `[label]`) |
| commands run, by id | the participant's name (a code: P1, P2, …) |
| how many keys were pressed, and modifier shortcuts | which characters were typed |
| the SEQ and SUS answers, and the moderator's observation codes | free-text notes (the moderator keeps those on paper) |

- **Local:** the data stays in the browser and leaves only as the JSON file
  the moderator saves. The recorder makes no request.
- **Deletion:** *Delete session data* removes it, and anything left on the
  device is deleted after 30 days. The consent form promises that session
  files are deleted once the round's analysis is written.

## The analysis

`node scripts/usability-analyze.mjs <folder> --round 1` turns a round's
session files into a report:

- per task: success, success without help, median time, SEQ, errors and
  help opened;
- SUS per participant, and the mean with a 95% confidence interval.

With `--round 2 --findings …` it also checks the plan's acceptance criteria
against the findings file. With 5–8 people the numbers show a direction,
not statistical significance.

The Hebrew SUS wording is the study's own translation, not a validated one.
It compares rounds with each other; comparisons with published SUS norms
are approximate.
