pages.title: Data-safety drill
pages.description: Every way Lumen saves a note to a folder, driven through kill -9, a full disk, lost permissions and another program editing at the same time, with a report per release.
pages.md:
The drill checks the claim that a note is never half-saved. It drives
**each way Lumen writes a note to a folder** through four kinds of trouble,
on a real disk with real processes:

| Trouble | What happens |
|---|---|
| **kill -9** | A process saves notes as fast as it can and is killed with `SIGKILL` at a random moment, 1,000 times |
| **Full disk** | A note grows until a save no longer fits on a small file system (`ENOSPC`) |
| **Lost permission** | The folder and its notes become read-only in the middle of saving |
| **Another program** | An editor or a sync client saves the same notes (temporary file, then rename) while Lumen saves |

Each saved version carries a SHA-256 of its own text. After every round each
note must be **one whole version**, no older than before, and still there.
A save that fails must fail loudly, so the app keeps the text and tries
again.

The save paths it drives are the phone folder (`src/storage/vault/mobile.ts`,
the real code), the OPFS worker that Safari before 26 uses, the desktop app's
write in `src-tauri/vault/src/lib.rs` (its algorithm; `cargo test` checks the
Rust itself), and the atomic save of plan W1.5 when the checkout has it. The
browser's File System Access path is atomic by design and is covered by the
e2e matrix (`e2e/data-safety.spec.ts`).

## Run it

```sh
npm run drill:data-safety -- --kills 1000 --full-disk /mnt/small
```

`--full-disk` takes a small file system you mounted for the test (on Linux:
`sudo mount -t tmpfs -o size=256k tmpfs /mnt/small`); without it the full-disk
part is skipped. Run as root, the saving process drops to an unprivileged
user so the permission test means something.

The report goes to `reports/data-safety-drill-<commit>.md` and `.json`, one
per release. The exit code is 0 only when no note was damaged or lost.

pages.title: Allowed image hosts
pages.description: See which sites may always load images in your notes, and revoke one or all of them.
pages.md:
An image from another site tells that site you opened the note. So Lumen
doesn't load it until you say so: the preview shows a placeholder with
**Load** (this image, until you reload the page) and **Always allow**
(every image from that site, in this browser).

## The list, and revoking

Command palette → **Privacy: allowed image hosts…** lists every site you
chose **Always allow** for.

- **Revoke** next to a site: its images wait for you again, at once — the
  preview shows the placeholder and nothing more is requested from that
  site. Images from it you loaded once with **Load** in this session are
  blocked again too.
- **Revoke all** does it for every site.

The list is kept in this browser (localStorage), not in your notes or your
vault, so another browser or device has its own.

The desktop app loads no images from other sites at all; there is nothing
to allow there.

pages.title: Journalist mode: redaction and locked notes
pages.description: Text you redact is removed from every export, not covered. A note can be locked with a password of its own.
pages.md:
Reporters, lawyers and researchers keep notes about people who must not be
named. Lumen has two tools for that, on top of [photo metadata
removal](/security/photo-metadata/).

## True redaction

Select the text and run **Redact selection** from the command palette. The
text is wrapped in `<redact>…</redact>`: you still see it in your note,
shaded, and it is **removed** from every export — PDF, print, DOCX, HTML,
Markdown, RTF, LaTeX, EPUB, slides and the rest. In its place the export has
`█████`, always five blocks, so the length of a name gives nothing away.

This is not a black box drawn over text that is still there (a well-known
leak in PDFs: copy the box, or run `pdftotext`, and the text comes back).
The exporters never receive the text at all.

The rules fail closed:

- A `<redact>` that is never closed removes everything after it, and every
  footnote too: the preview shows the footnotes at the end of the note, so they
  are shaded with the rest.
- A mark with attributes or a slash (`<redact class="x">`, `<redact/>`) is a
  mark too, exactly as the preview reads it, so what you see shaded is what
  goes.
- **Redact selection** over text that already has marks makes one mark over
  the whole selection; nothing that was covered before is uncovered.
- Photos inlined as `data:` URLs are judged by their bytes, whatever their
  label, and so are photos embedded in an SVG: a JPEG, PNG or WebP loses its
  metadata, and one that can't be cleaned (HEIC, AVIF) is left out.
- Marks count inside code blocks too.
- A `</redact>` that the preview doesn't read as one (in code, in a link's
  address, in a comment, or while a paragraph or table opened inside the
  passage is still open) doesn't end the passage. Everything the preview
  shades is gone from the export, and sometimes a little more. A suggestion
  (`{>>comment<<}`, `{~~old~>new~~}`) is read the way the preview reads it,
  so its `>` doesn't end a tag that the preview keeps open.
- The same goes for Markdown structure. A `<redact>` on a line of its own
  shades the blocks after it, and a `</redact>` typed inside one of them (a
  list item, a quote, a table cell, a heading or a paragraph) doesn't end the
  passage. To end it, put the `</redact>` on a line of its own, after a blank
  line:

  ```markdown
  <redact>

  - Source A
  - Source B

  </redact>
  ```
- Exports also leave out hidden text a reader of the file could find: HTML
  comments (`<!-- … -->`) and Obsidian comments (`%% … %%`).
- **Print** (⌘P) of a note with redactions goes through the same export.
- **Publish site** (GitHub Pages or a .zip) and the command line (`lumen publish`,
  `lumen convert`) go through it too: the pages, their titles and the site's search
  index never hold a redacted passage, and the photos they copy lose their metadata.

What it does not do: the note itself keeps the text (that is the point), so
syncing or sharing the *note* shares the text. Redact before you export, and
share the export.

## A note with its own password

Run **Note password…** on a note saved in the vault. The note is encrypted
with a password of its own, separate from the vault's: on disk, in sync and
in backups it is ciphertext, with one line saying how to open it.

pages.title: Monitoring and web vitals
pages.description: Error reports are off by default and sent only with your consent; web vitals never leave your device.
pages.md:
Lumen measures how fast it is on your device, and can send crash reports
to an error tracker, but only after you turn them on. Both work the same
way in every build.

## Web vitals: measured here, never sent

Lumen measures five page-speed metrics with the browser's
`PerformanceObserver`:

| Metric | What it is | Good |
|---|---|---|
| LCP | Largest Contentful Paint: when the largest visible element appears | ≤ 2.5 s |
| FCP | First Contentful Paint: when the first content appears | ≤ 1.8 s |
| TTFB | Time to First Byte: when the server's first response byte arrives | ≤ 800 ms |
| INP | Interaction to Next Paint: the slowest interaction this session | ≤ 200 ms |
| CLS | Cumulative Layout Shift: how much the layout jumps without your input | ≤ 0.1 |

The values stay in memory on your device. Open them with **Runtime
metrics** in the status bar, or from the command palette. They are never
sent, even when error reports are on. A sample stores no page address.

## Error reports: off by default

Lumen sends error reports only when **both** of these are true:

1. **You turned them on.** Click the **Telemetry** pill in the status bar.
   It is off in a fresh install. Click it again to turn reports off.
   Turning them off takes effect at once, even for an error that is
   already being reported.
2. **The build names an error tracker** in `VITE_SENTRY_DSN`. This can be
   Sentry or a self-hosted GlitchTip, which speaks the same protocol.

If either one is missing, the Sentry SDK is never downloaded and no
request is made. The default build has no DSN, so it makes no monitoring
requests at all. An e2e test (`e2e/monitoring.spec.ts`) checks this.

### What a report contains

Each report is rebuilt from a short allowlist before it leaves the browser:

- the error's class name, such as `TypeError`;
- the script file names, functions and line numbers of the stack trace;
- the app's release and environment, and the SDK's name and version.

The error **message is never sent**. A message can contain a title or a
line of a note without quotes ("Failed to save Quarterly plan"), and no
filter can reliably tell that apart from the app's own words. The stack
trace shows where the error happened, and that is enough to find it.

A report never includes:

- the error message, or any text logged with it;
- the page address;
- breadcrumbs, such as clicks, console lines and requests;
- user or IP data (`infer_ip: never`);
- tags, extra data or contexts.

There is no session replay, no performance tracing and no session
tracking.

### Every report is in the privacy ledger

Error reports go through the privacy ledger (command palette → **Privacy
ledger**) like every other request that leaves the device. Each one is listed under its own
category: "Error report — only with your consent, content removed". The
ledger shows where the report went, its size and its status. Under the
**local-only** AI policy, reports are refused before they leave, and each
refusal is listed as blocked.

## For operators: setting the DSN

Set the DSN at build time:

```bash
VITE_SENTRY_DSN=https://<public-key>@o123.ingest.sentry.io/4567 npm run build
# Docker: docker build --build-arg VITE_SENTRY_DSN=… .
```

**A DSN is not a secret.** Sentry designs it to be public: it ships in
every page that uses Sentry, and it only lets a client *submit* events
to one project. It can't read data. So a build-time `VITE_*` variable is
the right place for it, and secret scanners may ignore it.

The DSN's host is added to the CSP `connect-src` **automatically at build
time**, through the same mechanism as the other deployment endpoints
(`src/build/cspEndpoints.ts`). That covers the `index.html` meta tag,
`dist/_headers` and the nginx image. On **Vercel**, `vercel.ts` adds the
same origin to the header it serves, from the project's `VITE_SENTRY_DSN`
environment variable. No error-tracker host or wildcard is in the
checked-in policies.

## בעברית

- **מדדי ביצועים (Web Vitals)** נמדדים במכשיר שלך ולא נשלחים לשום מקום.
  אפשר לראות אותם בחלון "מדדי ריצה" בשורת המצב.
- **דוחות שגיאה כבויים כברירת מחדל.** הם נשלחים רק אם הפעלת אותם בכפתור
  "טלמטריה" בשורת המצב, **וגם** הבנייה כוללת כתובת DSN של שירות מעקב.
- הדוח כולל רק את סוג השגיאה ואת מיקומה בקוד. הודעת השגיאה, תוכן הפתקים,
  הכותרות והנתיבים לא נשלחים. אין הקלטת סשן ואין מידע מזהה.
- כל דוח מופיע ביומן הפרטיות. במדיניות "מקומי בלבד" הדוחות נחסמים.

pages.title: Mutation testing
pages.description: How Lumen checks that the tests of its security-critical code, such as encryption, the keyring, sync merges and the privacy ledger, really catch bugs.
pages.md:
Coverage tells you which lines ran, not whether a test would notice if they
were wrong. Mutation testing checks that. It plants small bugs in the code,
one at a time, and runs the tests each time. A test suite that still passes
with a bug in place has missed it.

## What is tested

The pure modules whose bugs would hurt most:

- **Encryption primitives:** ChaCha20-Poly1305, BLAKE2b, scrypt and Argon2id.
- **age** file encryption, and the **keyring** that holds the vault keys and
  devices.
- The **sync engine**: conflict merging, the manifest and blob headers.
- The **privacy ledger**, which records and blocks anything that would leave
  the device.
- The **secret store** (API keys and tokens: encrypted in the browser, or in
  the OS keychain on desktop), the **raw-HTML sanitizer** of the preview,
  Hebrew **text matching**, file **encryption**, **ZIP** import limits, and
  the **agent runtime**.

The list is in `scripts/mutation/targets.json`.

## The bugs it plants

| Kind | Example |
|---|---|
| Operators | `+` ↔ `-`, `<` ↔ `<=`, `===` ↔ `!==`, `&&` ↔ `\|\|`, `<<` ↔ `>>`, `^` → `&` |
| Constants | `n` → `n + 1` (`1` → `0`) |
| Booleans | `true` ↔ `false` |
| Negation | `!x` → `x` |
| Conditions | `if (c)` → `if (!(c))` |

Only code is mutated, never types, imports or comments. A mutant that
doesn't parse is left out. A mutant counts as **caught** when a test that
passes on the real code fails, when the run crashes, or when it hangs.

## Running it

```sh
npm run test:mutation                          # all modules, fails under 70%
node scripts/mutation/run.mjs --module keyring # one module
node scripts/mutation/run.mjs --max 200        # a bigger sample per module
```

The report, with the score per module and every surviving mutant's line, is
written to `reports/mutation/`. The plan's target is a score of at least
70% per module. A mutant that survives in a security module should get a
test that catches it.

pages.title: Photo metadata
pages.description: Photos you paste or drop into a note lose their GPS position, time, device and text metadata before they are stored.
pages.md:
A photo from a phone or a camera usually says **where** it was taken (GPS),
**when**, on **which device** (make, model, sometimes a serial number) and
sometimes **who** took it. If you share the note, export it or sync it,
that information goes with the photo.

Lumen removes it the moment you paste or drop a JPEG, PNG or WebP into a
note, before the image is stored in the vault or put inline:

- **Removed:** EXIF (GPS, date and time, camera, owner), XMP, IPTC,
  comments, PNG text and time chunks, Content Credentials (C2PA), and
  anything else the image doesn't need to be drawn. Only a fixed list of
  parts that draw the image is kept.
- **Kept:** the pixels, exactly as they were (nothing is re-compressed), the
  colour profile, and the photo's orientation, so a portrait photo still
  stands upright.

Lumen decides what a photo is from its contents, not from its name or the
type the browser reports. A JPEG named `.jfif` is cleaned like any JPEG.
A HEIC or AVIF photo (an iPhone original, even one named `.jpg`), and a
TIFF, can't be cleaned in place. Lumen redraws it through the canvas when
the browser can read it. Otherwise the photo is not added. GIF and SVG
images are stored as they are.

**When a photo can't be read:** the cleaning fails closed. A JPEG, PNG or WebP
whose structure Lumen can't parse is re-drawn through the browser's canvas,
which keeps only the pixels. If that isn't possible either, the photo is not
added (you see a message), and an export or a published site leaves it out.
Anything stored after the image's end is removed too: a second image (MPF,
used by some phones for depth or a preview) or the video of a motion photo.

**On export too:** photos already in the vault (including ones added before
this cleaning existed) are inlined clean into PDF and HTML exports, and
photos inlined in the note as `data:` URLs are cleaned in every export.
Publish site and `lumen publish` copy photos clean, whatever their file
names. They leave out HEIC, AVIF and TIFF photos and videos, whose metadata
(a video's location, for example) they can't remove, and list them as not
published. The file in the vault itself is not changed.

To keep the metadata (for example, for your own photo archive): **Settings →
General →** "Keep photos' location, time and camera details". Importing a
settings file never turns this switch on by itself.

On export too: photos already in the vault (including ones added before this cleaning existed) are inlined clean into PDF and HTML exports, and photos inlined in the note as data: URLs are cleaned in every export. Publish site and lumen publish copy photos clean, whatever their file names. They leave out HEIC, AVIF and TIFF photos and videos, whose metadata (a video's location, for example) they can't remove, and list them as not published. The file in the vault itself is not changed. To keep the metadata (for example, for your own photo archive): Settings → General → "Keep photos' location, time and camera details". Importing a settings file never turns this switch on by itself.

pages.title: A privacy report you can prove
pages.description: Export the privacy ledger as a signed report, check it with a script, and see the results of the outside audit for every version.
pages.md:
"Private" is a claim. Lumen lets you check it. The privacy ledger lists
every network request Lumen's features make. You can export it as a
**signed report**, check that report with a script, and compare it with
what an **outside network analyzer** saw during the same run.

## Export the report

⌘K → *Privacy ledger…* → **Export signed report**. The file covers this
session, from when the tab opened. For each request it says:

| | |
|---|---|
| Who | Which feature (its category and reason: "Anthropic (Claude)", "Model download", …) |
| When | The time |
| Where | The host |
| How much | Bytes sent and received, and whether it was allowed or blocked |

The summary (requests, how many left the device and to which hosts, bytes)
is computed from those entries. The file holds no prompt, note or header.

It is signed in the browser with **Ed25519**, using a key made on this device
the first time you export. The private half stays in IndexedDB and can't be
exported. The signature uses the minisign format, so both the script below
and the `minisign` tool can verify it.

## Check a report

```sh
node scripts/privacy/verify-report.mjs lumen-privacy-report-….json
node scripts/privacy/verify-report.mjs report.json --local-only          # also: nothing left the device
node scripts/privacy/verify-report.mjs report.json --pub device.pub      # pin the signing key
node scripts/privacy/verify-report.mjs report.json --extract out/        # then: minisign -Vm out/report.json -p out/report.pub
```

The script checks the signature and the trusted comment (which names the
report's SHA-256), and that the report is in its canonical form. It checks
the shape of every entry: times inside the session and in order,
`leftDevice` following the ledger's rule. It then **works the summary out
again** and refuses a report whose summary disagrees with its entries.
Without `--pub`, it proves the file hasn't changed since it was signed. With
`--pub`, it also proves which device signed it.

## Audit mode

The ledger normally lists AI traffic. In **audit mode**
(`localStorage["lumen.privacy.audit"] = "1"`) it also lists every other
request that leaves the device and the LAN, as *Other request*. Those are
listed but never blocked. The app is then run through an outside analyzer:

```sh
node scripts/privacy/audit.mjs --sign ~/.lumen-release/lumen-release.key --publish
```

1. **mitmproxy** (`mitmdump`, 10.1 or newer) records every request,
   including the app's own requests to the dev server, which proves it was
   in the path.
2. `e2e/privacy-audit.spec.ts` runs the journey under the **local-only**
   policy with cloud keys set to tempt every fallback: the views, an export,
   the AI commands, and a hand-made cloud request (which is blocked). It then
   exports the signed report and keeps Playwright's own request log.
3. The script verifies the report and compares it with **both** observers.
   The audit passes only when each observer saw traffic, nothing it saw
   leaving is missing from the report, nothing the report lists is missing
   from the wire, and **0 requests are non-local**.
4. `audit.json` is signed with the [release key](/security/supply-chain/)
   and published below.

## Results per version

Every version since the first audit has its row. `publish.mjs --check`
fails when a released version (in `CHANGELOG.md`) has no audit file in
`security/privacy-audits/`.

<!-- audits:start -->
_No audit published yet: the first runs with the first release after this page._
<!-- audits:end -->

## Store privacy labels

`store/privacy-labels.json` is the source for the App Store's *App Privacy*
answers and Google Play's *Data safety* form:

- **Data not collected.** With default settings nothing leaves the device,
  which is what the local-only audit shows.
- **Crash data, only on one condition:** the build has a crash-reporting key
  and the user hasn't opted out. It isn't linked to the user and isn't used
  for tracking.
- Every optional feature that can send something, mapped to its category in
  the ledger.

A test keeps the labels in step with the ledger's categories, the crash
reporter and the published audits.

pages.title: Secret scan of the build
pages.description: Why no secret may be a VITE_* variable, the gate that fails a build that sets one, and the scan of the live deployments.
pages.md:
Vite copies the value of every `VITE_*` variable the app reads into the
public JavaScript. Anyone who opens the site can read it. So a token, an
API key or a password must never be a `VITE_*` variable. Lumen enforces
this in three places.

| Where | What it checks | What fails |
|---|---|---|
| The build (`vite build`) | Every `VITE_*` variable set in the environment or in an `.env` file | A name not on `security/vite-env-allowlist.json` |
| The Vercel preview gate (`npm run secrets:dist`) | Every file in `dist/` | A token shape, or an inlined `VITE_*` value not on the allowlist |
| The live scan (`npm run secrets:scan-live`) | Production, the 3 newest previews, and the `VITE_*` names set in Vercel | The same, plus a `VITE_*` name in Vercel that is not on the allowlist |

The code rules in `npm run hygiene` keep secret-named reads (`…TOKEN`,
`…SECRET`, `…KEY`) and reads of `import.meta.env` as a whole object out of
`src/`. Before #243 such a whole-object read put **every** `VITE_*`
variable of the build into the bundle, even ones the app never used. The
allowlist gate covers that case too: a build cannot set a name that is not
listed.

## The allowlist

`security/vite-env-allowlist.json` lists each name a build may set, with
the reason it is public: a worker URL, an OAuth client id, a price id, a
public key. Names that start with `VITE_VERCEL_` are Vercel's system
variables (the deployment id, the git branch and commit). They are not
secrets, and the app reads none of them. A value that starts with
`ci-canary-` is a test canary and is allowed under any name.

To add a variable, add its name and the reason it is public. If it is a
secret, it does not belong here: keep it in the secret store
(`src/lib/secretStore.ts`) or on the server.

## What the scan looks for

- **Secret** (the scan fails): OpenAI and Anthropic keys (`sk-`), GitHub
  tokens (`ghp_`, `github_pat_` …), Google API keys (`AIza`), AWS access
  keys, Stripe live keys, Slack tokens, private-key bodies, JWTs other
  than a public anon key, and inlined `VITE_*` values not on the allowlist.
- **For review** (listed only): hex strings of 32 or more characters, and
  anon JWTs. Content hashes and embed ids look the same.

A report never shows a whole value. It shows the first 4 characters and
the length.

## Running it

```bash
npm run secrets:self-test        # plants a token of each kind in a temporary build and finds it
npm run secrets:dist             # scans dist/ after npm run build
VERCEL_TOKEN=… VERCEL_PROJECT_ID=prj_… VERCEL_TEAM_ID=team_… \
  npm run secrets:scan-live -- --report scan.md
node scripts/secrets-scan-live.mjs --url https://lumen-md.vercel.app
```

The live scan reads the **names** of the project's environment variables
from the Vercel API. It never asks for a value to be decrypted. For a
protected preview, set `VERCEL_AUTOMATION_BYPASS_SECRET`.

## If a secret was a VITE_* variable (15.18)

1. Treat it as public. Any build that ran while it was set may have put it
   in the bundle, and old deployments stay online.
2. Revoke it with the provider and create a new one.
3. Delete the `VITE_*` variable in Vercel (and in Netlify or CI, if used).
4. Put the new value where it belongs: the secret store for a user's key,
   or a server-side secret for a worker.
5. Run `npm run secrets:scan-live` and keep the report.

If no secret was ever set as `VITE_*`, record that, and 15.18 is done.

pages.title: Supply chain
pages.description: Fuzzed decoders, a reproducible build, an SBOM and offline-signed checksums for every release — and how anyone can check them.
pages.md:
The [threat model](/security/threat-model/) assumes the code you run is the
code that was released. Four checks make that verifiable.

## 1. The decoders are fuzzed

Everything Lumen reads from a file, a link, the clipboard or a plugin goes
through a decoder: the Markdown pipeline, front matter, BibTeX, JSON and
JSONL (Code Doctor, Insights), URLs (sanitizer, embeds, the CSP check), text
direction — and `.base`, `.excalidraw`, PDF annotations and plugin
manifests as those land.

```bash
npm run fuzz                                    # 1,000,000 inputs per decoder
node scripts/fuzz/run.mjs --target bibtex --runs 50000
node scripts/fuzz/run.mjs --target bibtex --seed 1 --from 4242 --runs 1   # replay one input
```

Inputs are built from each format's own pieces (with Hebrew, Arabic, bidi
controls, emoji and lone surrogates), then cut, repeated and nested
thousands deep. Each decoder runs in its own worker: an exception it does
not document is a **crash**; one input running over a second is a **hang** —
the worker is stopped and the run continues. Failing inputs are saved to
`fuzz-findings/` with the command that replays them. The pass criterion is
0 crashes and 0 inputs over 1 s.

`--engine fast-check` runs the same decoders through
[fast-check](https://fast-check.dev) (with shrinking) once it is installed.

**Pathological Markdown (plan W4.16).** The first run found seven inputs
(8–14 KB) that took 0.5–2.8 s to render: thousands of `[` or `]` in one
paragraph, or lists nested 231 levels deep, make the parser's work grow with
the square of the text. A note like that would freeze the editor. Now a
block (the text between blank lines) with more than 256 brackets or more
than 32 nesting levels is shown as raw text, in a code block, exactly as
written (`src/renderer/boundMarkdown.ts`). Every real note stays far inside
both bounds and renders as before. The live preview also shows a block as
raw text once its render took more than 200 ms. The seven inputs are pinned
in `src/__tests__/markdownSlowInputs.test.ts` (each under 50 ms).

## 2. The build is reproducible

```bash
npm run repro
```

builds the same commit twice from clean (with `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` set to
the commit time) and compares the SHA-256 of every file in `dist/`. Any
difference is listed by file.

A release build has no source maps (plan 11.5), and the check fails if one
appears, so there is no map that could differ between two builds. Maps are
for a local investigation only (`LUMEN_SOURCEMAP=1`):
`node scripts/supply-chain/repro-check.mjs --sourcemap` builds with them and
says which fields of each differing map differ.

## 3. Every release has an SBOM

```bash
npm run sbom          # → release/sbom.cdx.json
```

A CycloneDX 1.5 list of every npm package (`package-lock.json`) and every
Rust crate (`src-tauri/Cargo.lock`): version, package URL, the lockfile's
hash and the licence. Same lockfiles, same bytes.

## 4. Every release is signed — offline

The signing key belongs to the release owner and never enters a CI system.

**Once** (on the owner's machine):

```bash
LUMEN_RELEASE_PASSPHRASE=… node scripts/supply-chain/keys.mjs --out ~/.lumen-release
cp ~/.lumen-release/lumen-release.pub security/release-key.pub   # commit this file only
```

Keep `lumen-release.key` and its passphrase offline (a password manager
and a second offline copy). Old releases stay verifiable with the old
public key if the key is ever replaced.

**Each release:**

```bash
npm run repro && npm run build
LUMEN_RELEASE_PASSPHRASE=… npm run release:sign -- --key ~/.lumen-release/lumen-release.key \
  --artifact <each desktop / mobile file>
```

This writes `release/SHA256SUMS` (every file of `dist/` and each artifact),
`release/sbom.cdx.json` and a minisign signature of each, then checks the
result. Upload the four files with the release.

**Anyone can check a release:**

```bash
npm run release:verify                      # signatures + every file against SHA256SUMS
# or with the standard tools:
minisign -Vm SHA256SUMS -P <public key from security/release-key.pub>
sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS
```

The signatures are standard minisign (Ed25519 over BLAKE2b-512), made with
Node's own crypto — no extra package.

## OpenSSF Best Practices

The [OpenSSF Best Practices badge](https://www.bestpractices.dev) is
claimed by the project owner. What it asks for, and where it is:

| Criterion | Here |
|---|---|
| Public repo, licence, contribution and security-report docs | `LICENSE`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, `SECURITY.md` |
| Version-controlled, unique version per release, release notes | git tags, `CHANGELOG.md`, `RELEASE.md` |
| Automated tests and a test policy for new code | vitest + Playwright; every task's Definition of done |
| Static analysis and dependency scanning | ESLint, CodeQL, `npm audit`, `cargo audit`, gitleaks (`.github/workflows/security.yml`) |
| Dynamic analysis (fuzzing) | `npm run fuzz` |
| Signed releases, reproducible build | `npm run release:sign` / `release:verify`, `npm run repro` |
| A vulnerability report process with response times | `SECURITY.md` (acknowledged within 48 h, a fix timeline within 5 business days, 90-day disclosure) |

pages.description: window.__lumen.agentReview exists only in development and tests.
pages.md:
The end-to-end tests drive a few app functions through `window.__lumen`.
One of them, `window.__lumen.agentReview`, stages a change for the
[agent review screen](/ai/agents/) the way an agent's write tool does. A
page script that could call it could put changes in front of you that no
agent proposed, so it is **not part of the app you install**.

## Where it exists

| Build | `window.__lumen.agentReview` |
|---|---|
| `npm run dev` (Vite dev server) | yes |
| `npx vitest` (unit tests) | yes |
| `VITE_LUMEN_TEST_SURFACE=1 npm run build` (the e2e-prod job only) | yes |
| `npm run build` (every release, the PWA, desktop and mobile) | **no** — the code is removed from the bundle |

The release build replaces `import.meta.env.DEV` and
`VITE_LUMEN_TEST_SURFACE` with constants, so the surface and the function
behind it are dropped when the bundle is minified.

## Checking a build

```sh
npm run build
npm run check:test-surface
```

`check:test-surface` reads every JavaScript file under `dist/` and fails if
one still sets or reads `.agentReview` (the translation keys such as
`agentReview.title` are text and do not count). CI runs it after the
production build.

pages.title: Threat model
pages.description: What Lumen protects, from whom, at each of its boundaries — vault, sync, sharing, plugins, agents and the web clipper — and where each defence is tested.
pages.md:
Privacy is Lumen's central claim, so it has to be checkable from the
outside. This page names, for every boundary where data crosses from one
party to another, the threats in each STRIDE category (**S**poofing,
**T**ampering, **R**epudiation, **I**nformation disclosure, **D**enial of
service, **E**levation of privilege), what stops them, and what is left.
Each defence points to the code or test that holds it; a row without one
is a known gap.

## What is protected

- **Notes and attachments** — the vault (browser storage, a folder, the
  phone).
- **Secrets** — AI keys, Git and cloud tokens, room passwords
  ([Secrets and encryption](/security/vault/)).
- **What the user types into AI** — prompts and the notes sent with them.
- **The app itself** — the code a user runs must be the code that was
  released ([Supply chain](/security/supply-chain/)).

## Who we defend against

| Attacker | Can | Cannot (assumed) |
|---|---|---|
| A malicious note or file (shared, imported, clipped, synced) | Put any bytes in a note, a `.canvas`, a front-matter block, a link | Run code outside the sandboxes |
| A network attacker / a relay or signaling server | Read and change traffic it carries | Break TLS or AES-GCM |
| A cloud provider (Dropbox, Drive, Gist) | Read, change, delete or hold back the files it stores | — |
| A plugin or live block | Run its own code in its sandbox | Reach the page's origin, the vault or the network without a granted capability |

| | Threat | Defence | Where |

| T | A path from a note, a zip or git leaves the vault (`../`) | Every path checked: no `.`/`..`/NUL segments; Rust checks the folder again | `src/storage/vault`, `src-tauri/vault` tests |
| I | A desktop WebView script reads other files | The WebView has no `fs:` permission; only the app's `vault_*` commands, inside the picked folder | `src-tauri/capabilities` |
| D | A huge or malformed file hangs the app | Decoders fuzzed: 1,000,000 inputs each, no crash, nothing over 1 s | `npm run fuzz` |

| | Threat | Defence | Where |

  click-only behaviour needs.

  PDF annotations and plugin manifests join it as those modules land.

pages.title: Trusted repositories
pages.description: Let agents propose changes in a git repository you own without the extra outside-content question.
pages.md:
Notes that come from a **git clone or pull** are *outside content*:
someone else may have written them, and they may hide instructions for
an agent (see [Local agents → Outside content](/ai/local-agents/#outside-content-prompt-injection)).
So when an agent has read such a note, every change it proposes asks you
first, before it is even staged.

For a repository that is yours, such as your own notes repo or a repo
only your team pushes to, that question gets in the way. **Trust this
repo** turns it off for that repository.

## Turn it on

1. Open the command palette (⌘K) and run **Trusted repositories…**
   (group *Security*).
2. Every repository cloned in this browser is listed with a switch. All
   of them start as **Asks first**.
3. Turn the switch on and confirm. The repository is now **Trusted**.

The setting is saved **on this device only**. It is not synced, not
written into the repository, and not shared with collaborators.

## What changes

With the switch on, when everything outside in an agent's run comes from
trusted repositories:

- a change the agent proposes is **staged without the extra question**;
- the change still **waits for your review** in the staged changes list.
  Nothing is written until you apply it.

## What stays the same

- The repository's notes are still **delimited and cleaned** in the
  prompt, and the run still records that it read outside content.
- **Web requests still ask** (fetch a page, search the web): that is how
  text planted in a note could send your data out.
- Anything else outside in the same run asks as before: a clipped page,
  an imported folder, a web result, another repository that is not
  trusted, or a note in the trusted repository whose frontmatter says
  `untrusted: true`.

## When trust is dropped

Trust belongs to the repository you looked at, so it is removed when:

- you **clone again** into the same folder;
- you **rename or move** the repository folder, or move another folder
  onto its name.

Moving notes *inside* a trusted repository keeps it trusted. Turn the
switch off at any time to make agents ask again.

## Who should not use it

Anyone who can push to the repository can put text in front of your
agents. Do not trust a repository with outside contributors, a fork of
someone else's project, or a repository whose push access you don't
control.

pages.title: Usage on this device
pages.description: Lumen counts starts, commands and errors on your device only. The weekly report is off until you turn it on, and you send it yourself. Nothing leaves without your click.
pages.md:
Lumen has no analytics and no tracking. To know whether the app is used and
what breaks, it keeps a few **counters on your device**. They never leave
it unless you send them yourself.

## What is counted

Per day, in the browser's local storage (`lumen.usage.v1`):

| Counter | What it holds |
|---|---|
| Starts | how many times the app opened |
| Commands | how many times each command ran, by its id from the app's code (`file.exportHtml`, `help.feedback` …) |
| Errors | how many uncaught errors happened: one number, no message, no stack, no file |

The counters hold no note text, no file names, no user or device id and no
time of day. A counter name has to look like a command id: no spaces, no
slashes, no runs of digits or capitals. Anything you typed can't become one.
Commands named after something in your vault are counted under one fixed
name each: every installed template as `template.apply`, every recent file
as `recent.open`, every plugin command as `plugin.command`. So a template
called after a source never shows its name.
The last 60 days are kept.

## The dashboard

**Help: Usage on this device** in the command palette shows:

- the day you started using Lumen
- how many of the last 7 and 30 days you used it
- whether you came back after a week and after a month
- the most used commands, and how many commands went unused for 30 days

There you can turn counting off, which also clears the counts, or clear them
at any time.

## The weekly report: only when you send it

The dialog shows the whole report as JSON, exactly as it would be sent. It
holds counts only: the app version, the week, days used, retention, starts,
errors, the 20 most used commands of the app, and the number of unused ones.

- **Open on GitHub** opens a new tab with a GitHub issue form that has the
  report in it. Nothing is sent until you submit that form yourself. The
  click is listed in the [privacy ledger](/ai/privacy/) with its size.
- **Copy** puts the JSON on the clipboard.
- **Remind me once a week** is off by default. When you turn it on, a
  notice appears once a week with a button that opens the dialog. The notice
  sends nothing.

Without one of these clicks, Lumen makes no request for usage. The tests
check this (`src/__tests__/usageMetrics.test.ts`): counting, errors, the
dashboard and the report make 0 requests and add 0 ledger entries. A report
built after secrets were planted in the vault's storage contains none of
them.

pages.title: Vault encryption at rest
pages.description: Encrypt the whole vault where it is stored — OPFS, a real folder or the desktop folder — with a passphrase, a recovery key and auto-lock.
pages.md:
Optional. **Command palette → Vault encryption…** encrypts every note and
file of the vault where it is stored, so a copied browser profile, a lost
laptop or a synced folder shows only ciphertext. Lumen asks for the
passphrase when it opens the vault.

> **Read this before you turn it on.** An encrypted vault can't be read as
> plain text by Obsidian, git, a text editor or any other program — only by
> Lumen with the passphrase or the recovery key. If you use the same folder
> with other tools, keep the vault unencrypted (or keep a plain export).

## What is encrypted

| Where | How |
|---|---|
| Every file of the vault — notes, attachments, canvases, `.trash/`, `.git/` | AES-256-GCM, one random nonce per write, on every storage: the browser's own storage (OPFS), a real folder you picked in the browser, the desktop app's folder |
| History snapshots (the backups the Version History panel shows) | AES-256-GCM in IndexedDB |
| Agent traces (the last 50 runs, which include parts of notes) | AES-256-GCM in IndexedDB; migrated when encryption is turned on, deleted when it is turned off |
| Semantic search index (embeddings and the text of each chunk) | AES-256-GCM in IndexedDB |
| AI answer cache | Not written while the vault is encrypted; emptied when encryption is turned on or off |
| The open note and the open tabs, which Lumen normally keeps in `localStorage` to resume a session | Not kept; after a reload you open the notes again from the vault |

The fast search index lives in memory only and is never stored.

**Not encrypted:** file and folder names, file sizes and dates (the vault
stays a normal folder of files); the list of recent files; API keys and
tokens (they have their own store, see [Secrets and encryption](/security/vault/));
the encrypted sync's own state; version history of live collaboration rooms;
results of batch AI jobs; what the learning critic remembers. A vault export
(zip or folder) is plain text on purpose.

## Passphrase, recovery key, lock

- **Passphrase** — at least 12 characters. The key is derived with
  **Argon2id** (RFC 9106), memory-hard so guessing on graphics cards is
  slow. Lumen picks the most memory this device opens within a second:
  46 MiB in one pass, or 19 MiB in two on a slower device (OWASP's
  options). It runs in Lumen's own code, with no extra library, and is
  checked against the RFC's test vectors. A vault made before this, with
  PBKDF2-SHA256 (600,000 iterations), still opens and stays on PBKDF2,
  including when you change the passphrase. To move it, choose **Switch to
  Argon2id** under Vault encryption. Update Lumen on every device that
  opens the vault first: an older Lumen refuses an Argon2id vault (it
  doesn't misread it), so Lumen never switches on its own. Only the small
  header file is rewritten.
- **Recovery key** — 30 characters (150 random bits), shown **once**, when
  you turn encryption on, before anything is encrypted. Lumen goes on only
  after you confirm you saved it. The vault's key is derived from it, so it
  opens the vault even if you forget the passphrase *and* even if the
  vault's encryption header files were lost. Case, spaces and dashes don't
  matter when you type it back.
- **Lock** — after 15 minutes without a key press or a click (choose 5, 15,
  30, 60 minutes or never in the dialog), or **Lock now**. A locked vault
  covers the app with the unlock screen; nothing is read or written until it
  is unlocked, and saves made meanwhile go on afterwards.
- **Change passphrase** re-wraps the key; no file is re-encrypted.

## Safety: what happens if something goes wrong

- **Wrong passphrase** — refused; nothing is read or written.
- **Turning it on or off is cut off** (tab closed, battery, crash) — each
  file is converted copy-first: the new version is written next to it,
  read back and checked, and only then replaces the file. Every file is
  always either complete plain text or complete ciphertext, and Lumen reads
  both. **Check and repair** finishes the job.
- **A file changed by another program meanwhile** is left alone and done by
  the next run. A file that doesn't decrypt with this vault's key is
  reported and never overwritten or deleted.
- **The header** (`.lumen-encryption.json`, plus `.lumen-encryption.backup.json`)
  is written twice; one damaged copy is fine. It is removed only when no
  encrypted file is left. If both are gone, the recovery key brings the
  vault back.
- **A plain file dropped into the folder** reads normally and is encrypted
  by Check and repair.
- An encrypted vault can't be **moved** to another place (the move would
  copy decrypted notes): turn encryption off, move, turn it on again.

## Turning it off

**Vault encryption… → Turn off encryption** asks for the passphrase again,
then decrypts every file back to plain text. History comes back in the clear;
agent traces and the semantic index are deleted (they are rebuilt).

Update Lumen on every device that opens the vault first: an older Lumen refuses an Argon2id vault (it doesn't misread it), so Lumen never switches on its own. Only the small header file is rewritten. Recovery key — 30 characters (150 random bits), shown once , when you turn encryption on, before anything is encrypted. Lumen goes on only after you confirm you saved it. The vault's key is derived from it, so it opens the vault even if you forget the passphrase and even if the vault's encryption header files were lost. Case, spaces and dashes don't matter when you type it back. Lock — after 15 minutes without a key press or a click (choose 5, 15, 30, 60 minutes or never in the dialog), or Lock now . A locked vault covers the app with the unlock screen; nothing is read or written until it is unlocked, and saves made meanwhile go on afterwards. Change passphrase re-wraps the key; no file is re-encrypted.

sections.heading: Safety: what happens if something goes wrong
sections.text: Wrong passphrase — refused; nothing is read or written. Turning it on or off is cut off (tab closed, battery, crash) — each file is converted copy-first: the new version is written next to it, read back and checked, and only then replaces the file. Every file is always either complete plain text or complete ciphertext, and Lumen reads both. Check and repair finishes the job. A file changed by another program meanwhile is left alone and done by the next run. A file that doesn't decrypt with this vault's key is reported and never overwritten or deleted. The header (.lumen-encryption.json, plus .lumen-encryption.backup.json) is written twice; one damaged copy is fine. It is removed only when no encrypted file is left. If both are gone, the recovery key brings the vault back. A plain file dropped into the folder reads normally and is encrypted by Check and repair. An encrypted vault can't be moved to another place (the move would copy decrypted notes): turn encryption off, move, turn it on again.

sections.heading: Turning it off
sections.text: Vault encryption… → Turn off encryption asks for the passphrase again, then decrypts every file back to plain text. History comes back in the clear; agent traces and the semantic index are deleted (they are rebuilt).

pages.title: Secrets and encryption
pages.description: How Lumen stores API keys and tokens, and how to encrypt a document.
pages.md:
Lumen keeps the secrets it needs — AI provider keys, Git and cloud tokens,
the collaboration room password, the research search key — out of plain
browser storage. The whole vault can also be encrypted with a passphrase and
a recovery key — see [Vault encryption at rest](/security/vault-encryption/);
the secrets described here are kept apart from it.

## Where secrets live

| Where Lumen runs | How secrets are stored |
|---|---|
| Browser / installed web app | Each secret is encrypted with AES-GCM-256 under a WebCrypto key that is **non-extractable**: no script can read out the raw key bytes. The secrets no longer sit in localStorage as plain text, so a glance in DevTools, a localStorage dump or a synced settings export shows only ciphertext. |
| Desktop app on macOS / Windows | The operating system's keychain (Keychain / Credential Manager). Lumen keeps only the secret names, so it knows what to load. |
| Old engines without IndexedDB or WebCrypto | Plain localStorage, as before. Lumen reports this mode instead of hiding it. |

**Honest limits:**

- The key is stored in the same IndexedDB database as the encrypted
  secrets, and Lumen decrypts them at startup without asking for a
  password. Someone who copies the whole browser profile and opens it in
  Lumen can therefore use the stored key and read the secrets.
  Non-extractable stops the key from being *exported*, not from being
  *used*. Protecting against a copied profile needs a password you type
  (planned with whole-vault encryption, task 11.4) or the desktop app's
  OS keychain.
- Code running inside Lumen's own origin could also ask WebCrypto to
  decrypt. The Content Security Policy and the HTML sanitizer are what
  keep foreign code out.

Plain-text secrets left by older versions are encrypted and moved at startup.

## Encrypting a document

`⌘K → 🔒 Encrypt Document` encrypts the open note with AES-256-GCM under a
password you type. The note is replaced by an encrypted block; `Decrypt
Document` restores it. Lumen does not keep the password — lose it and the
note cannot be recovered.

## What is not encrypted

Your notes themselves are plain Markdown files (in the browser's private
file system, or a folder on desktop). Encrypting the whole vault at rest is
planned as an option (plan task 11.4).

pages.title: Self-hosting with Docker
pages.description: Run Lumen on your own infrastructure with the docker-compose bundle.
pages.md:
> Lumen is a **local-first** editor — by default everything runs inside
> your browser, no servers needed. This guide is for teams who want to
> own the persistence layer (collab, billing, audit log) on their own
> infrastructure.

## What's in the bundle

`docker-compose.yml` brings up five services on a single VM:

| Service | Port | What |
|---|---|---|
| `lumen-web` | 80 | nginx serving the React SPA + strict CSP — the same image as the Fly deployment (`Dockerfile`, `deploy/nginx.conf`) |
| `lumen-signal` | 4444 | y-webrtc signaling — peers find each other |
| `lumen-collab` | 4445 | Persistent Hocuspocus server (SQLite + backups on the `collab-data` volume; health: `/healthz`) |
| `lumen-billing` | 4446 | Stripe webhook handler (optional) |
| `postgres` | 5432 | Entitlements + audit log (collab does **not** write here — a Postgres snapshot archive is not implemented) |

A collab volume (`collab-data`: SQLite + its own hourly backups) and a Postgres volume (`postgres-data`)
persist outside container lifecycles.

## Prerequisites

- A Linux VM with **2 vCPU + 4 GB RAM** (Hetzner CX22, DigitalOcean
  basic-2, AWS t4g.medium are all fine)
- **Docker 24+** and **Docker Compose v2**
- A domain pointing at the VM (we'll use `lumen.example.com` below)

## 5-minute install

```bash
# 1. Clone Lumen
git clone https://github.com/talstilkol/lumen-md.git
cd lumen-md

# 2. Copy + edit the env template
cp .env.onprem.example .env.onprem
$EDITOR .env.onprem
#   set LUMEN_PG_PASSWORD to a strong value
#   set LUMEN_BASE_URL to your domain
#   leave LUMEN_COLLAB_TOKEN empty for now (see the note below)
#   leave Stripe / Sentry / WorkOS empty for now

# 3. Build + start
make onprem-up
```

After ~60 s of image build + container start, visit
`http://<vm-ip>` and you should see the Lumen editor.

:::caution[`LUMEN_COLLAB_TOKEN` in this bundle]
The bundle passes `LUMEN_COLLAB_TOKEN` to the collab server, but not to the
app it builds (the root `Dockerfile` has no `VITE_YJS_WEBSOCKET_TOKEN`
argument), and the app has no screen for entering one yet. With a token
set, the app's own clients are refused by the collab server. Keep it
empty, or build the web image yourself with `VITE_YJS_WEBSOCKET_TOKEN`
(see [Persistent rooms](/collab/persistent/)). New rooms are end-to-end
encrypted either way.
:::

## DNS setup (recommended)

Point these subdomains at the VM:

```
lumen.example.com    A    <vm-ip>
signal.example.com   A    <vm-ip>   # or proxy via lumen-web
collab.example.com   A    <vm-ip>
```

Then put a TLS terminator (Caddy, Cloudflare Tunnel, or your existing
nginx) in front. The bundled nginx serves HTTP only; the ports are
mapped 1:1 so a reverse proxy can terminate SSL upstream.

Serve Lumen from the root of its own (sub)domain, as above. The
security headers that ship with the app (the bundled nginx config,
`public/_headers` and `deploy/vercel.base.json`) match root paths. If you build with
a sub-path `base` such as `/app/`, prefix those routes yourself,
including the Web Playground's `/playground-runner.html`, `/assets/*`
and `/playground/*` rules. Without them the playground preview is blocked.

Every host runs the Web Playground, including Netlify (an edge function
gives the runner page its own headers there). What works where, and the
`LUMEN_RUNTIMES=slim` option for a smaller image, are in
[Where Lumen runs](/self-hosting/hosting/).

## Optional: Billing

If you want to gate Pro features (persistent collab, semantic search,
fine-tune AI) behind a paywall, add Stripe credentials and re-up with
the `billing` profile:

```bash
# In .env.onprem
STRIPE_SECRET_KEY=sk_live_xxx
STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET=whsec_xxx

# Bring up with the billing service
docker compose --env-file .env.onprem --profile billing up -d
```

The billing worker runs `wrangler local-mode` so the same code that
powers the Cloudflare deployment also runs in your VM.

## Optional: Sentry telemetry

Build the web image with `--build-arg VITE_SENTRY_DSN=https://<key>@<host>/<project>`
(Sentry or a self-hosted GlitchTip) to make error reports available. They
stay **off** until a user turns them on with the Telemetry pill in the status
bar; note text, titles and paths are removed first, and each report is listed
in the privacy ledger. The DSN's host is added to the CSP at build time. A DSN
is public by design, not a secret. See [Monitoring and web vitals](/security/monitoring/).

## Optional: SSO with WorkOS

Set `WORKOS_API_KEY=…` and `WORKOS_CLIENT_ID=…` to enable SAML / OIDC
sign-in. A workspace admin pastes their IdP metadata URL into Settings
→ Organisation; WorkOS handles the protocol dance.

## Daily ops

| What | Command |
|---|---|
| Tail logs | `make onprem-logs` |
| Restart everything | `make onprem-down && make onprem-up` |
| Check Postgres | `docker compose exec postgres psql -U lumen` |
| Hard reset (deletes all data) | `make onprem-reset` |

## Backup

The two Docker volumes are the only state Lumen owns:

```bash
# Postgres dump
docker compose exec postgres pg_dump -U lumen lumen | gzip > lumen-pg-$(date +%F).sql.gz

# Collab volume (collab.sqlite and backups/; the server also keeps hourly backups itself)
docker run --rm -v lumen_collab-data:/data -v "$(pwd)":/backup alpine \
  tar czf /backup/lumen-collab-$(date +%F).tar.gz -C /data .
```

User documents themselves never leave the browser — they live in OPFS
(Origin Private File System) per browser, per origin. Encourage users
to back up their local content with `⌘K → Export the whole vault…`
(see [Export and import](/workspace/export-import/)).

## Updating Lumen

```bash
git pull
make onprem-up   # rebuilds images + restarts containers
```

Database migrations run automatically on container start
(`docker/postgres-init.sql` is idempotent).

## Sizing for scale

Single-VM 2 vCPU / 4 GB handles:

- Up to ~50 concurrent collab rooms (LevelDB hot cache)
- ~1k entitlement reads / sec
- Linear cost on audit volume — every mutation writes one row

For larger deployments, split:

- `lumen-web` + `lumen-signal` on one VM (stateless, horizontally
  scalable)
- `lumen-collab` on a dedicated VM with a persistent EBS / Block-Storage
  volume
- Postgres on managed RDS / Cloud SQL

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Likely cause |
|---|---|
| 502 from `lumen.example.com` | reverse proxy can't reach `lumen-web:80` |
| Editor loads but collab silently fails | `lumen-signal` not reachable; check WS upgrade rules in proxy |
| Pro features stay locked | `lumen-billing` not in the compose profile, or webhook signature secret wrong |
| `pg_isready` fails | `LUMEN_PG_PASSWORD` mismatch between `.env.onprem` and the volume |

If something else breaks, `make onprem-logs` is your friend — the
five-line per-service prefix makes it easy to spot the offender.
